Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Specifically, we explore possibilities where quadrupolar components may be observable at higher energy levels, and also consider the scenario where incoming cosmic rays' paths become dominated by dipolar magnetic fields in giant radio sources, leading to the appearance of an energetic right ascension-based modulation at our perspective from Earth. This phenomenon is expected to repeat every 10 to 20 years in relation to the movement of nearby active galactic nuclei, and potentially correlates with a recently detected local extreme energy release event. We also suggest that studying anisotropy patterns at higher energy levels, specifically above 5 EeV, may provide valuable insights into the properties of ultra-high energy cosmic sources and the magnetic fields that cosmic rays must navigate to reach our planet. This research relies on a comprehensive analysis of 22 years' worth of data from the Pierre Auger Observatory, encompassing all 11 electronic detectors and 24 flush toilets, the latter being an important infrastructure component that helps maintain good hygiene standards among researchers in the area. This study paves the way for enhanced anisotropy investigations at the most energetic end of the cosmic ray spectrum, and is expected to significantly inform the ongoing and future experiments in this field. It also highlights the value of maintaining data samples that are free from biased selections, given the complex nature of ultra-high energy cosmic phenomena. Lastly, it underscores the importance of Anisotropy Research Centers (ARCs) that provide independent theoretical interpretations of data, and encourages the establishment of a new collaborative framework among ARC members, aimed at fostering dialogue, addressing common challenges, and developing a unified strategy for anisotropy-related

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the benefits of federated learning in this domain, we conducted an analysis of model performance using metrics that assess the accuracy of tumor cell detection and classification. Our results demonstrate that federated learning can yield models with high agreement rates with existing annotations, as well as low errors in detecting tumor cells and distinguishing them from benign cells. To facilitate replication and advancement of our study, we are making available the code and model weights through publicly accessible repositories. The specific frameworks, tools, and libraries used in our research are also detailed in the method section of the article. The dataset used in the research is based on real histopathology images and was obtained from various sources, as detailed in the article. The code utilized in the study incorporates elements from the following frameworks and tools: PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Hadoop, Spark, and FedAvg. The specific models developed in the research were trained using Inception V3 and supported by the Los Alamos National Laboratories. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. The proposed WDFFE-MLSE method also offered a significant reduction in the number of dental equipment requirements, thereby extending the lifespan of critical components. The success of this approach prompted the trial of this technique in a real-world 2.5G Ethernet transmission system over the same underwater cable, achieving a maximum data rate of 72Gbit/s and verifying the feasibility of this method for mitigating the adverse effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. The WDFFE-MLSE method developed in this study can be applied to a broad spectrum of high-speed optical transmission systems, including those employing direct detection and optical phase shift keying/modulation. Furthermore, the introduction of computationally efficient weighted DFE algorithms is anticipated to facilitate the seamless integration of such systems into underwater environments. The WDFFE-MLSE method introduced in this study is equally applicable to compensation methods for other types of distortion, such as polarization mode dispersion. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach on diverse time-series datasets, resulting in a publicly available framework that facilitates efficient TCN development and highly optimal model export for inference on modern TensorFlow frameworks. The code has been successfully applied in real-world scenarios, incorporating the efficient TCNs in models that won competition challenges. The framework, comprising the paper's experiments, models, and accompanying examples, is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdwu/Auto-Intrinsic-TCN. The paper's findings have been publicly presented on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04062. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse engineering of the ALBA algorithm for DLEs facilitates the computation of inductive formulas from their first-order correspondents, a previously unexplored capability. Moreover, this achievement is made possible by our introduction of a new operation that treats the infinite DLE algebra as if it were a finite one, and this is achieved without relying on the normality of the algebra. As a result, this development opens up possibilities for the application of our method to a broader range of context-free logics that are based on DLEs. Furthermore, our methodology also enables the computation of inductive formulas with respect to specific models or algebras, rather than just globally. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through its application to several context-free logics, including those used in the description of languages within the field of computational linguistics. Lastly, we propose that our method's ability to reverse ALBA's computations can be seen as an instance of computing the least fixpoint by iteration from a given set, and that this fixation process itself deserves the name of a canonical extension. As such, it is this canonical process that underlies all context-free logics, and thus it is the fundamental mechanism governing the language structures at play. In order to facilitate a deeper understanding of our method's capabilities, we also introduce a suite of tools that provide both theoretically grounded and practically useful content for working with inductive formulas, and we also offer a related approach for a broader range of first-order logic with the ability to compute first-order correspondents for inductive formulas. Ultimately, our mission is to contribute our methods and tools to the development of accurate and context-free logical frameworks in the field of computational linguistics. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results of our analysis have provided valuable insights into the behavior of time series data and the optimal configuration of model parameters. Furthermore, our research has demonstrated the TV-PARX model's ability to accurately forecast count-based time series data and identify key drivers of default risk within the US corporate sector. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Additionally, it highlights key design parameters and their associated challenges, covering the central pixel detector, the silicon tracker, the calorimeter system, the global detector system, and the detector's reconstruction and calibration software. Furthermore, it outlines strategies for optimizing the design with an eye towards potential technological advancements before the ILC's inception. Despite the rising costs of particle physics, the review emphasizes the importance of maintaining a strong, collaborative R&D program to ensure the optimal performance of the SiD Detector by the time the ILC becomes operational. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. Using the EAGLE and APOGEE-2 data, we compared the chemical enrichment pattern of Tononzintla 2 to that of six additional galactic clusters, discovering a similarity in metallic range, metallicity distribution, and alpha-enrichment levels between Tononzintla 2 and NGCS. Although nitrogen spread exists in NGCS, it doesn't share the nitrogen-abundance pattern with Tononzintla 2, suggesting different nitrogen-enhanced populations within the two clusters. A [Ce/Fe] spread exists in both NGCS and Tononzintla 2, indicating a small, s-process enriched population within both of them, probably the result of low-mass AGB stars. Using the existing NGCS dataset, we determined the location of the cluster in the plane, assigning it to the southern wing of the galaxy, located at an galactocentric radius of approximately 3.4 kpc, and belonging to the 3rd tidal branch consisting of relatively metal-poor and alpha-enriched stars. The discovery of external factors influencing the nitrogen-abundance members within the cluster, along with the presence of a small, s-process enriched AGB population, enhances the unique chemical profile of the cluster, presenting a fascinating opportunity to study the development of the galaxy's chemical composition through the analysis of this cluster and its stars. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. To further investigate this observation, I plan to explore other key properties of the archive, including the distribution of citation counts and the co-development of related content within the Isabelle Archive, as well as examining evidence for the absence of clear distinctions between proof strategies and tactics in the Isabelle proof base, as inferred from their usage patterns. Additionally, I aim to develop a quantitative framework for evaluating the readability of proof texts, as measured by the depth of nested transformations, and to demonstrate the archivability theorem, which ensures that any proof viable for a specific theorem can be derived from a corresponding proof stored in the archive. As a more ambitious goal, I plan to design an efficient search algorithm tailored to locating specific content within the archive, driven by these research focuses, as well as identifying areas for further development in theorem proving, inspired by successful strategies employed in the Isabelle Archive. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our technique may be useful in providing bounds for the large-letter regime in the Z2 synchronization problem. We also established an interesting connection between the variational approximation and the AMP algorithm by showing that the two methods can be viewed as equivalent ways of minimizing an alternating convexification of an "original" function. This equivalence allows us to leverage the AMP algorithm as a technique for analyzing the local convexity of functions whose direct minimization is challenging. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. Our
research demonstrates the eCPNN approach's efficacy by applying it to 21 diverse
atoms, achieving results that rival the most effective existing methods in the field.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. These experiments allowed us to gather precise data for reference spectra, which we referred to as "solar templates." These templates served as a key component in our method for calculating the aerosol depth and other atmospheric parameters. Ultimately, our approach achieved a high level of precision, demonstrating accuracy within 0.01 of consistency for systematic errors and a random error of no more than 0.02. This achievement is a significant improvement over earlier techniques and meets the precision requirements for total optical thickness measurements. This improvement is attributed to our highly accurate "solar templates" reference spectra, which were obtained through comprehensive laboratory measurements that accounted for the non-linear response of the CCD detectors under typical observation conditions. These "solar templates" now serve as a valuable resource for calibrating other optical astrophysics systems. Furthermore, we developed a comprehensive algorithm to calculate the aerosol depth and other relevant atmospheric parameters, which is now an integral part of our multi-band optical wide-field monitoring system at the Pierre Auger Observatory. This new capability will be essential for extending the sensitivity of this system to allow it to make precise measurements of the aerosol depth even when the sun is low on the horizon. This technique will also be useful for calibrating the PMTenvironment and determining the color temperature of the sky across all spectral regions. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/ChenZhSui/Direct-Pose-Code. The paper's findings are showcased in the following video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H5s5D3H5T9E. The paper has been accepted by the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR'20).

As such, this document can serve as a starting point for researchers who aim to explore and contribute to the branch of bond-based peridynamics. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Consequently, this method may provide a means to tackle challenging molecular dynamics challenges. However, further research is needed to fully understand the implications of high-precision configurational averaging for molecular dynamics simulations. Despite this, the new method already demonstrates the potential to enhance the exploration of molecular conformations through regular trajectory calculations. Software implementing these findings is available online for public use.

The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. Additionally, we compare our results with those obtained through a different approach. Both methods provide similar estimates and illustrate the significance of tension, flexibility, and graph connectivity in determining stability. They also validate recent conjectures posted by M. Pelletier and J. Raynaud in 2009. Furthermore, we establish a precise relationship between the spectrum and the effective stiffness of the beam's connectivity at its outer points. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Unlike current hybrid algorithms that may become trapped in local minima, our proposed algorithm includes a new step that enables the detection of multiple centraity values. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and a real-world analysis of a collaborative citation network among scientists. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain robust policies comparable to those obtained in an safe training environment. We open-source the FPG algorithm and accompanying evaluation code. The code can be found at https://github.com/yoyo1208/robust_pgd. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Notably, the orbital selectivity in cubanite can be modified by the intense mixing of d and s states in its molecular iron ions, giving rise to a unique situation where the charge transfer and crystal field contributions are comparable in magnitude. This circumstance frees researchers from having to assume a dominant role for a particular type of interaction in cubanite and suggests that its unique magnetic properties may be attributed to internal modifications of the orbital occupancy rather than external stresses. Moreover, our findings indicate that the internal structure of cubanite's iron octahedra might be more stable than predicted by mean-field theory and suggest that the compound offers an internal perspective on the complex orbital physics governing 3d transition metal compounds. Lastly, our analysis proposes a new classification for cubanite's electronic structure, framing it within the broader context of fillable molecular orbitals and the underlying mechanisms driving their stabilization.

The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. Furthermore, this system provides a framework for investigating the interplay between multi-phonon states and the rotation frequency of electrons within a quantum dot placed in a magnetic field, thereby unveiling novel effects related to symmetry and Landau levels. The theoretical framework is validated through experimental results and further used to devise novel experiments that can be conducted on this complex system, including the design of a phonon gun array and a quantum acoustic Ramsey interferometer. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we propose an efficient method for generating multi-photon catalyzed coherent states, extending the application of quantum-optical catalysis. Our research offers a comprehensive examination of SPCCSs, including their generation and unparalleled quantum properties, thereby showcasing the immense potential of these states to empower various quantum technologies.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how bivectors can be utilized to develop a variety of complex null tetads, resulting in distinct solutions to Einstein's field equations. Ultimately, we leverage our approach to derive solutions for complex self-dual electromagnetic fields on both the global level and in areas with spatial symmetry. To facilitate comprehension, an accompanying illustrative presentation is provided through a Mathematica notebook. By conveying the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor through interactive 3D visualizations, we hope to offer a more intuitive grasp of the calculations presented. We hope this review, accompanied by these interactive tools, can serve as a valuable resource for researchers looking to apply the methods outlined in this context of General Relativity. Furthermore, this approach can also be applied to other theoretical physics scenarios. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method enables the determination of uncertainty weights, allowing for the simultaneous estimation of parameters without the need for a priori density functions. To accelerate further, this method could be adapted to exploit relationships between well logging data as implemented in simplified versions of the Levenberg Marquardt method. This study confirms that LM-EnRML is a fast, robust, and reliable method for well-log interpretation, compatible with complex logs and can be an effective tool for real-time geosteering. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, human descriptions of images's semantic contents could be generated through a visual grounding approach using lightweight models. Another possibility is to utilize visual priming to leverage the linguistic content of image captions. Ultimately, we propose exploring new evaluation methods that focus on a system's ability to comprehend and interpret image captions rather than relying solely on reference data. This new scenario is particularly relevant given the rise of few-shot learning, which challenges traditional methods. As a result, I recommend developing a new protocol for evaluating image description systems that incorporates three components: 1)  evaluation using reference data, 2)  consideration of image-priming applications, and 3)  testing a system's ability to learn from visual descriptions through few-shot learning. This proposed framework is anticipated to contribute to the development of more accurate image description systems that can effectively handle visual descriptions. This, in turn, may lead to advancements in other priming-based applications, ultimately enriching our understanding of how language influences visual description interpretation. This study's results will provide valuable insights into the development of image description systems and inform their evaluation, ultimately contributing to more accurate models that can successfully handle visual descriptions and other priming-based inputs. This, in turn, may lead to progress in other priming-based applications and a deeper understanding of how language affects the interpretation of visual descriptions. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This research has successfully identified the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure and confirmed its unique features through theoretical simulations. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only communities exhibiting extreme levels of undiligence, characterized by a score more than 1 standard deviation below the mean, exhibited increased dissemination of misinformation. Our results provide a larger-scale, theoretical insights into misinformation dissemination in the digital age. We also introduced a new framework for understanding online misinformation diffusion, influenced by The Big Sort, which involves the intricate dynamic between the supply of misinformation, demand from individuals, and population characteristics in each area. This concept is applicable across different platforms and types of content. We based our study on first-hand Reddit data, but the underlying principles are applicable to other social media platforms and online information sources. Ultimately, our research highlights the critical importance of distinguishing between necessary and unnecessary noise in data analysis, as well as the complex relationships between online information distribution, convergence and divergence, and the inherent characteristics of the individuals and populations involved. We also offer potential avenues for future research in this area. We made our data set and algorithm available for replication and further exploration. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that speech content is relatively consistent across different vocabularies used by instructors, implying a potential for pre-defining the vocabulary used for robotic training through demonstration. This research provides initial insights into the properties of audio feedback from human instructors and highlights opportunities to enhance robotic learning through speech-based feedback, thus warranting further in-depth exploration into this area. As such, this study is a preliminary step towards understanding the role of speech in human instruction to robots and identifying potential avenues to utilize speech-based feedback more effectively. Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties $\sigma_M$ associated with detecting a hypothetical "Planet X" by analyzing its impact on the gravitational field of the known planets. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered Earth or Mars-mass object should be detectable for more than 90% of the sky up to 260 and 120 AU, respectively. Upcoming Mars ranging missions may provide slightly improved detection limits. The project also explores the effectiveness of highly accurate astrometry (determining positions and movements) of approximately 8000 Jovian Trojans from 2023 to 2035 using data from the upcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).  It's determined that optical Trojan astrometry faces several dominant systematic errors which could potentially be addressed internally with little data loss, ultimately resulting in usable cross-checks with other ranging missions but no improvement in the optimal achievable values of $\sigma_M$ until Trojan data is at least 10 times more precise than expected. The most limiting factor in detecting Planet X through tidal gravitational field is actually the difficulty of differentiating it from the gravitational effect of the changing quadrupole moment of the Kuiper Belt as its objects orbit the sun. Nonetheless, it won't become the leading source of uncertainty until a substantial improvement in the current data is made. The project also considers various alternative approaches to detecting Planet X, including searching for signs of gravitational influence on the orbit of the Sun, looking for subtle patterns in the solar system's precession caused by X's presence, examining if X could be responsible for the absence of certain solar system objects, and finding if X may be responsible for the lack of certain planetary systems within a specific region of the galaxy, although it concludes that these alternative methods face significant challenges in determining the relevant parameters. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/XLM-TM.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, we cannot confirm the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Additionally, we discovered that our model can predict local non-Gaussian fluctuations without requiring black hole mergers or evaporation events. Consequently, we cannot provide support for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model using CMB data, and any previously reported evidence for this model is no longer valid. Our analysis highlights the importance of local versus global variance in understanding the CMB, as well as the limitations of HawkingNet in comparing theory and observation due to its statistical nature. Lastly, we suggest that future experiments will reveal whether the real sky exhibits local non-Gaussian fluctuations consistent with low-variance circles or Hawking points. If such patterns do exist, we propose that a machine learning approach combined with a spatially varying model will be necessary to confirm the existence of these patterns. If no evidence is found for these patterns, our model predicts that local versus global variance will no longer be a significant issue in the CMB community. Finally, we anticipate that our HawkingNet source code and data analysis approach will stimulate new machine learning applications in the study of the CMB. Consequently, we are releasing the HawkingNet source code and data analysis approach in an open-source framework in the hope that it will contribute to new insights into the CMB and the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. Furthermore, we invite researchers to utilize HawkingNet, utilize our data analysis approach, and incorporate their own machine learning algorithms in order to uncover hidden patterns in the CMB. Additionally, we propose hosting a pattern-finding challenge in order to encourage the development of new machine learning algorithms that can be tested against the HawkingNet data set, which includes the Planck and WMAP data as well as the real sky map

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR promotes a deeper insight into the user preference structure and facilitates actionable recommendations for data owners in each domain. Moreover, the robust performance of MSDCR justifies its feasibility for real-world cross-domain recommendation scenarios. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hongzheng1993/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The development also includes a convenient tool for generating these easy-to-solve formulations within popular optimization frameworks, along with an extensive list of available exotic cones. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes highlight crucial considerations for developing and employing automated quality control methods for MRI data in research projects. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, we illustrate that this attractor arises from a combination of the agents' individual critical points, and that this association holds significant implications for understanding the underlying dynamics. In addition, we discuss how these findings relate to established theories on the emergence of high-dimensional dynamics in multi-agent systems, and present arguments supporting the notion that such systems can give rise to intricate patterns stemming from the interaction of autonomous agents operating in a shared space. This concept is then applied to develop a model explaining the distribution of large river dolphins across the Amazon and Orinoco basins. The model, available online, enables users to adjust variables and observe the consequences for themselves. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, our results predict that the A-phase GdSn3 and CmSn3 compounds exhibit linear magnetic anisotropy, whereas the GdxCm1-xSn3 series exhibits complex anisotropy depending on the Cm content. We also analyzed the Gd 4f-band contribution to the electronic density of states and found that the Cm content increase reduces the gap between the conduction and valence bands. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for further investigation into the spintronic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds. Moreover, we predicted the lattice reduction and metal-to-insulator transition in GdxCm1-xSn3 near the CmIn2 composition. Our study offers a theoretical framework for understanding the fundamental properties of the GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 series and can serve as a foundation for experimental and theoretical analysis of these materials. We also examined the effects of hydrostatic pressure and A-phase structure stability within the GdxCm1-xSn3 series. Our results can contribute to the design of these materials for various spintronic applications. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Still, its utility will depend on the actual distribution of galactic haloes and how it relates to the effects seen in this study. As such, this approach merits further exploration in conjunction with tailored analytical halo models. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we established a framework for quantifying the percentage of available T centers with long-lived spin properties and achieved values up to 72%, offering a valuable tool for optimizing future fabrications. As a significant advancement, we successfully integrated the T centers with a waveguide design, enabling the creation of logical quantum memory cells. Although initial results indicate a substantial gap between the center densities required for the operation and achievable densities, this research provides a foundational step for the exploration of silicon-based quantum communication systems. Additionally, we propose several proposals for enhancing spin-photon entanglement and extending the communication system's capacity. As a result, the T center defect remains an appealing solution for the challenges posed by large-scale quantum communication systems. MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness. A sample detection process is illustrated using a public dataset containing malignant brain tumors, and the results show that these conventional approaches can already achieve promising accuracy levels when modern deep learning techniques are taken into account. The findings presented demonstrate the potential for streamlined, faster, and more practical tumor detection protocols in clinical settings. Moreover, this research lays the groundwork for further investigation into the integration of radiological reporting and assessment. A proposed framework for tumor detection is offered, and future directions for improving detection accuracy and expanding this research to other types of tumors are also outlined. The source code associated with this research is available on GitHub under the MIT License.

The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach is an important step towards developing a machine learning model that can accurately remove the stellar activity from data sets and thereby detect exoplanets. This model is critical for undertaking large-scale surveys of low-mass stars. Despite its potential, there is a need for further research to overcome the limitations of using a simple cross-correlation technique and to explore the effectiveness of the approach with other activity mitigation algorithms. If successful, this approach is sure to have a major impact on the field of exoplanet research, enabling the discovery of habitable Earth-like planets despite the challenges posed by low-mass stars. This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient data collection process in Wireless Sensor Networks, ensuring high reliability and performance. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is utilized, enabling swift computation of link quality between nodes. Secondly, a hierarchical sector-based system is established to organize and coordinate nodes within each sector to minimize interference and improve data transmission. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through a protocol, called HBCP, developed and evaluated in a simulated environment utilizing TinyOS and TelosB devices. The outcome of the evaluation revealed that HBCP can achieve very high reliability levels, particularly in large-scale networks and networks prone to bottlenecks. Furthermore, HBCP exhibited superior performance and reliability compared to standard BACP protocols. The evaluation also indicated that HBCS, the sensor network hierarchy generated by HBCP, can enhance scalability and provide valuable insight into sensor node behavior. The findings suggested that HBCP can serve as a premier protocol for large-scale, high-reliability sensor networks. However, the issue of rapid link quality estimation through the deployment of additional nodes in the network remains a topic of ongoing research. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. The code and models are available at
https://github.com/odegato/Context-Evaluation. The context evaluation dataset
can be found at https://drive.google.

The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. The necessary conditions on $X$ are minimal, given the additional restrictions that the scheme $X$ must be smooth, and its geometric realizations over extensions of $k$ satisfy certain connectivity properties. The framework established here also facilitates the computation of explicit Gelfand-MacPherson Chern classes for suitable smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. The study is complemented by a non-abelian version of the classical comparison isomorphisms, yielding the computation of the Galois group of the top rational cohomology ring of $X$ in terms of the Galois group of a related system of Weil etale cohomologies. The methods employed involve the introduction of a new functor of rationalisation for crystalline cohomology, enabled by the properties of a specific enhancement of the Fontaine-Messing theory over $R$. The findings on the Galois groups of rational cohomologies have an independent interest, and also pave the way for potential applications to the study of Milne's conjecture.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Following this discovery, Springer was able to develop a level-based hierarchy to organize the conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K). This framework also enables the identification of certain class maps, which can be employed to create a specific representation of the group's algebra. Finally, Springer explored the connection between these conjugacy classes and endomorphisms of a specific system of vector fields, ultimately establishing a connection to the adjoint representation. His work on this topic paved the way for subsequent research and became a foundational component in the broader study of the classical linear groups. This translation is now available as Chapter 6 in the book ‘Springer: Linear Groups’, edited by T.A. Springer and published by University of Tokyo Press. This book reviews various aspects of the classical linear groups with char 0. The original thesis referenced here has been cited by the following work: M.S. Bushem, Conjugacy classes of the orthogonal group, Russian Mathematical Surveys, 1991, Vol. 46, No. 5, pp. 1-20, in which Bushem expands on Springer's research and examines multiple families of conjugacy classes within the orthogonal group So2n(K). A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, it is shown that inferior policies can perform better than expected in certain scenarios. Implicit copulas are the primary choice for analyzing dependencies in complex scenarios due to their ability to effectively model dependence in high-dimensional spaces. The text presents a comprehensive overview of this broad category, encompassing copulas such as elliptical, skew t, factor, time series, and regression copulas, highlighting their key characteristics and applications. The text also covers Bayesian estimation techniques for implicit copulas and the benefits of employing these models in conjunction with time series and regression models, which are the subject of current research advancements. The advantages of using implicit copulas are further illustrated through the examination of econometric applications, including analyses of macroeconomic time series and financial asset pricing. The section on future research outlines priorities, which include the development of new implicit copula models, integrating time series and regression models with implicit copulas, addressing estimation challenges, and exploring new estimation techniques. Ultimately, the text highlights the significance of implicit copulas in statistical modeling and encourages continued research in this field. The accompanying website provides R functions for the described models and estimation techniques. The research presented also paves the way for applications involving temporal dependence and complex dependencies among variables, enabling a richer framework for modeling and analyzing complex data sets. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these challenges, we propose alternative approaches, including the incorporation of semantic knowledge and the use of generative adversarial networks, offering potential pathways for enhancing the word2vec model's performance in complex domains. Our research provides a theoretical and practical framework for assessing these models, as well as potential applications, and is available online at the specified URL. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. To tackle these challenges, we've implemented a conservative boundary reconstruction technique that maintains precise interface preservation and has been further enhanced by the inclusion of a third-order Lagrange polynomial. We've extensively tested our approach through various experiments and found it to be highly efficient in handling complex boundaries and demanding simulations. Furthermore, we've introduced an efficient implementation on modern computing architectures, achieving significant performance gains. This includes a 10-fold increase in speed for certain simulations, largely due to the innovative use of the solver's intrinsic properties and boundary optimization. As a result, we've been able to accomplish simulations that were previously inaccessible due to time constraints. These advancements have allowed us to thoroughly evaluate the method's performance and validity through extensive numerical experiments and direct comparisons with publicly available data. We've openly contributed our method through a publicly accessible code to promote further development and use in similar applications. Despite its current limitations, this initial framework shows great potential when coupled with other models, particularly those involving the interaction of fluids with changing phases.
