Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. A sentence's interpretation can now fluctuate (toggle) between these different interpretations, enabling the computation of probability estimates for each interpretation. This method supplements the traditional tensor product with an orthogonal spin state, enabling the simultaneous consideration of all sentence interpretations, and demonstrates its viability on a range of examples from the GLSA corpus. Moreover, our method achieves the probability estimates it computes organically, without necessitating any additional post-processing steps. This approach offers a valuable tool for further research on the resolution of derivational ambiguity. Despite its potential, our method still faces considerable challenges, as evident from the difficulty it has in tackling more substantial texts and the challenge of distinguishing interpretation toggling from true ambiguity. To address these issues, the proposal includes the experimental integration of multi-head attention mechanisms, along with the theoretical inclusion of time and the directional density matrix space's restriction to the type system's syntax space. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research provides the first concrete advancements in the domain of rationalizable learning in multiagent settings.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. Researchers were also able to show that by changing the model to only sever connections to infected neighbours, there will be a threshold where the model suddenly switches from no infections to finally reaching a steady state with a certain fraction of the population infected. That fraction of infection was found to be exactly 1/2 for the first infection rate, and there are sharp thresholds where the model switches between two completely different behaviours near that fraction. Finally, researchers were able to show that by changing the model to only sever connections to infected neighbours, there will be a transition where the model suddenly switches from no infections to finally reaching a steady state with a certain fraction of the population infected. That fraction of infection was found to be exactly 1/3 for the second infection rate, and there are sharp thresholds where the model switches between two completely different behaviours near that fraction. Researchers were also able to show that by changing the model to only sever connections to infected neighbours, there will be a transition where the model suddenly switches from no infections to finally reaching a steady state with a certain fraction of the population infected. That fraction of infection was found to be exactly 1/2 for the third infection rate, and there are sharp thresholds where the model switches between two completely different behaviours near that fraction. Finally, researchers were able to show that as the model is scaled to accommodate larger and larger populations, the probability of a person being infected will converge to a value that depends on the rate of infection and the rate at which connections are formed or broken, and this convergence happens regardless of how the model is changed. This convergence is relatively smooth for the first and third infection rates, but it will converge more suddenly for the second infection rate, where the model will switch from no infections to complete spread. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, this soliton becomes a genuine soliton if the manifold's Ricci operator has a specific characteristic structure. Additionally, this research proves that on 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton cannot exist if the manifold is of positive curvature. Lastly, this study establishes that a strong Cotton soliton cannot exist on almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds.

Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Given the significance of this task, a comprehensive integration platform for PDF research has been developed, leveraging the MHVPDF framework and encompassing numerous contributions to various physical processes, such as those to top quark production, studied in detail through explicit examples. In addition, this program provides an interactive command-line interface and graphical user interface options, enabling users to easily integrate theoretical predictions and evolve PDFs according to DGLAP equations in a scalable and efficient manner. As a result, this program serves as a valuable resource for PDF research, making it available under the MIT License at the following repository https://github.com/JulienGuillet/MHVPDF-Integration. In conjunction with the JaxRoost symmetry preservation framework, this program has also enabled the integration of certain NLO PDF contributors, showcasing its capability for complex calculations. As the program is highly modular, with all inputs and outputs represented by Python objects, integrating new contributors or processes involves simply modifying the relevant lists and functions, overcoming one of the significant hurdles in PDF research. By providing a unified framework for PDF research, with features like DGLAP evolution and research collaboration tools, this program is an invaluable resource for any researcher working on PDFs. As an added benefit, the development of this program has prompted the creation of several new contributors to PDF research, further enhancing its value. As the program continues to evolve, with numerous features yet to be integrated, along with the potential for improvement, it is an excellent example of an open-source project that can facilitate collaborative research in PDF physics. As such, it is hoped that this program will serve as a foundation for a broader integration platform, enabling researchers to collaborate more effectively and contribute to the advancement of PDF research. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Furthermore, the results show that the proposed approach adapts to varying target distributions and is robust to different scenarios of data sampling. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for correct assignment of the hole-like bands. Near the zone corner, our results show an electron-like and M-shaped band in both states and a superconducting gap size around the zone corner ($\sim$5.5 meV), contradicting previous findings. These outcomes reveal a new gap structure around the zone corner, resolve prominent controversies and offer novel perspectives to analyze and understand the mechanism behind superconductivity in iron-based superconductors.

Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. This equivalence is key to applying the superbosonization formula directly to broaden the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, thus enabling more efficient solution of certain matrix problems. As a result, we can derive novel exact expressions for specific self-averaged properties of broad classes of non-Gaussian matrix ensembles. Moreover, we showcase the application of this method using the Hamiltonian ensemble related to Wigner-Dyson symmetry, leading to the derivation of new explicit results for the density of Delone spectra, and we predict that this approach will be crucial for investigating other self-averaged properties in rotation-invariant matrices. Lastly, we highlight the potential for the superbosonization formula to solve more general matrix valuel problems when linked to quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. 

This finding is further supported by an analytical example involving a Hamiltonian with interacting boson modes, where the successful application of the superbosonization formula yields an unexpected exact result. As a consequence, we can obtain novel exact solutions for a broad class of matrix ensembles, and we believe this will enable the solution of more general matrix value problems when linked to quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Additionally, our (1/$T$) plots of the spin-lattice relaxation rates revealed a curvature in thicker samples, which can be attributed to a deviation from the Orstein-March ratio rule anticipated for a strong, direct coupling between spin and lattice in LaNiO$_3$. Notably, our findings demonstrate that even in thick LaNiO$_3$ layers, the spin-lattice relaxation rates exhibit a notable temperature sensitivity, ultimately requiring an interpretation beyond the standard activated behavior. Our results provide valuable insights into the microscopic characteristics of LaNiO$_3$ and highlight the significance of (NMR) spectroscopy in examining the correlated state of this material. Lastly, a comparison with LaFeO$_3$ LaFeO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices has revealed distinct spin-lattice relaxation patterns, suggesting that the fundamental mechanisms governing the correlated state of these transition metal oxides differ significantly. This study offers a comprehensive NMR analysis of LaNiO$_3$ and sheds light on the underlying physics of these materials. Through this research, we have obtained a deeper understanding of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$, a key component of various heterostructures, and have provided a stronger foundation for further exploration of the associated physics and material properties. This research has been conducted at the High Field Magnetic Laboratory of the National Institute of Materials Science (NIMS). The NIMS has provided financial support for this study. The LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices were prepared through pulsed laser deposition by T. Kawasaki and Q. Ghahramani. The LaFeO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices were prepared through pulsed laser deposition by H. Lee.

of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a

incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our findings demonstrate significant 
improvements over baseline generators in terms of conversational depth, diversity 
metrics, and overall quality as rated by human assessors. Our highly advanced 
models still fall short of human performance in long-term conversations but 
significantly outperform baseline generators and showcase substantial potential 
for further development. We have made our datasets and models publicly 
available, taking a significant step towards propelling the generation of 
conversational dialogue. Our code and models can be accessed at this website.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. As part of this work, we also create a suite of $f(R)$ gravity simulations that can be used to develop mock galaxy catalogs and emulators for the upcoming Euclid telescope survey. These simulations, encompassing a broad range of gravitational scaling factors and allowing for the evaluation of the impact of gravity models on galaxy survey analyses, are now incorporated into the AuDiT suite of initial conditions and mock catalogs. This work represents the first comprehensive attempt to create a diverse range of modified gravity simulations capable of being employed with galaxy survey data. As part of this work, we also present a new suite of $f(R)$ gravity simulations and incorporate the MiCroKNOs galaxy formation model to produce mock galaxy catalogs from these simulations. These catalogs are designed to aid in developing new tests capable of distinguishing between modifications of gravity and dark matter models. As a preliminary investigation, we create mock catalogs for the most extensively studied modified gravity theories, specifically $f(R)$ gravity, and then utilize these simulations to introduce two novel projects aimed at distinguishing between these theories and dark matter models. This work represents a computational breakthrough, achieving highly accurate modified gravity simulations through analytical approximations, and also marks a significant conceptual advancement, introducing several novel projections capable of distinguishing between modifications of gravity and dark matter models. As part of this work, we create extensive N-body simulations for a broad range of modified gravity models, incorporating multiple variations of $f(R)$ gravity and achieving highly accurate results through analytical approximations. These simulations result in highly precise modified gravity models and facilitate the development of mock galaxy catalogs and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. The reaction rate data, obtained from the model, were utilized to derive an empirical model that could predict the response of reaction rates to acoustic vibrations in different jet flames. The study concludes with recommendations to enhance the accuracy of reaction rate prediction by suggesting areas for further research in numerical modeling. To understand stellar vibrations, we created a mathematical framework to derive a specific frequency of oscillations. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. The framework's associations with existing CRDT designs are also clarified through a comparative analysis of its components and existing designs. Furthermore, the RWF is viewed as a bridge connecting the field of Replicated Data Types and Distributed Transaction protocols. As such, it is available under an permissive license to encourage widespread adoption and is readily accessible on GitHub under the name RedisRWF. The source code is also hosted on TPC.org. The RWF is believed to contribute positively to the growth of the CRDTs community by making it easier to develop new CRDTs. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. Additionally, about two-thirds of neutron star binaries enter quiescent states characterized by low field strengths, making them increasingly difficult to identify through radio pulses, particularly in later stages of binary evolution when the neutron star's spin rate accelerates. As a result, the estimated population of neutron star binaries within the Milky Way is substantially higher than previously thought, further diminishing the likelihood of finding stellar mass black holes in the galaxy's center through direct detection methods. However, to validate this finding, further observational data from radio pulse surveys are necessary to clarify the total population count of neutron star binaries and observe the predicted increase in radio pulse frequencies above 100 Hz. If confirmed, this study will have significant implications for further research into the galaxy's center's black hole population. It will also necessitate re-examination of existing data on low mass X-ray binaries, particularly in the galaxy's center, to distinguish between black holes and neutron stars as their primary components. The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, analysis based on using the line velocity method, with additional steps to eliminate potential anomalies by identifying and discarding 2 times standard deviations from the mean, reveals that no distinct deviation from Newton's gravitational law exists at a radius of around 10,000 astronomical units. 

Due to the relatively low uncertainty in velocity measurements, existing wide binary star data have nearly sufficient accuracy to differentiate between the principles of Newton's gravitational law and the Modified Newtonian Dynamics model using the line velocity approach. In contrast, to make the same distinction with projected sky velocities, data for around one thousand additional wide binary systems will be needed.

Furthermore, to accurately determine how gravitational forces work in this context, potential sources of systematic error must also be accounted for, including any hidden or unobserved companion stars within these wide binary systems and possible moving groups within these star systems, with control being achieved statistically by narrowing down and considering specific and scientifically supported parameters for these star systems and evaluating the theoretical models against their predictions. 

The most effective way to investigate the behavior of gravitational forces in this context would be to conduct a comprehensive analysis of all available wide binary star data, regardless of the distance or velocity range, with the goal of directly comparing these star systems to popular theoretical models that describe how gravitational forces work across this range. 

In addition, because the law of gravity at these low acceleration rates appears to be well-established and relatively certain, future experiments that test this law could consider focusing on a broader range of conditions, such as various types of star systems and different statistical analysis methods, to further explore the fundamental principles of gravitational forces. 

Finally, using the line velocity method and existing wide binary star data, no evidence could be found for any distinct deviation from Newton's gravitational law at a radial distance of around 10,000 astronomical units, despite previous claims to the contrary.

We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics.
The solution also highlights the significant difference in wave energy preservation
at large radii between head and tail shocks, with a potential greater impact on
matter ejection. This distinction emphasizes the importance of waveforms in
shock evolution.
We also predict shock behavior to transition from weak to strong and utilize
this to estimate mass loss in scenarios involving rapid sound pulses and minor
central explosions. Additionally, we anticipate that in scenarios involving large
explosions or near-Eddington limits, where radial shocks could become strong and
efficient at matter ejection, the mass loss might significantly exceed the
Eddington limit by a factor of ten. This theory could be tested with upgraded
telescopes capable of detecting super-Eddington outbursts. We propose that even
a small mass loss of $10^{-5} M_\odot$ yrs can be identifiable with the next
generation of spectrographic instruments. We also suggest that if future
observations can detect rare super-Eddington outbursts, they may provide valuable
insights into the physics of massive stars and their ultimate demise.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects. Our primary tool 
is the modularity of geometric globalization, as anticipated by Diamond--Sasaki, 
and this relationship holds true under the condition that the weight is not 
algebraic or when geometric modularity holds for an infinite number of algebraic 
weights. Furthermore, our methodology involves the use of Rankin--Shafere 
type constructions and their associated beyond-base-change principles. By 
combining these constructions and understanding the resulting Galois representations, we can determine representation properties such as geometric modularity or degeneracy, thereby establishing the connection between geometric modularity of non-algebraic or multiple algebraic weights. This research also includes new cases of Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview. Building on the foundational notes by Holm and Unger, we examine the role of $\tau$-tilting theory in the broader context of algebraic research, discussing its connections to other significant areas such as the Serre-Dessins problem, elliptic gradings, and the representation theory of Lie superalgebras. We also explore promising directions for future investigation in this field. Along the way, we cover key results and prove notable theorems, including a version of the Riemann-Hilbert problem for non-simple algebras and the application of $\tau$-tilting to representation theory of Lie superalgebras. These results demonstrate the powerful tools that $\tau$-tilting theory provides for understanding the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras and also reveal the potential for $\tau$-tilting to contribute to other areas of research. The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
artificial neural networks. Although widely adopted in other contexts, these methods 
have not been heavily employed for amplitude analyses. The article also introduces 
new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density 
estimation utilizing artificial neural networks. Furthermore, the article addresses 
issues of model selection, bias calculation, and statistical inference in such 
scenarios. Through simulated and real data, we evaluate the performance of these methods 
and their implications for density estimation. Ultimately, this article aims to 
encourage the exploration of innovative approaches to address instrumental influences 
in hadron decay studies.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study investigates the issue of determining the minimum number of nodes to split (possibly all) to obtain an edge-free representation. A 3-SUM variant has been identified as an appropriate proxy for evaluating the node splitting problem's computational complexity, and a proposed algorithm achieves optimal performance in this context, requiring only linear time. The algorithm's efficiency is further demonstrated across various input scenarios, including certain cases where specific nodes already lie on the same side of the two horizontal lines or where the corresponding entities' alignment is randomly distributed along the horizontal axis. As an added benefit, the optimal planar drawing resulting from the node splitting process can be obtained through a simple sorting step, followed by an animation-style transition to obtain the desired minimum-crossing planar drawing. The existing methods for generating connected bipartite graphs and testing their planarity can be used to further analyze the edge-free representation's connectivity. The proposed method's effectiveness is illustrated through several examples, and its source code is available for public review. The ideas presented in this study can also be applied to other types of graphs, and the associated challenges are discussed. The concept of using node splitting as a 3-SUM proxy is believed to offer an innovative approach to addressing computational complexity issues in graph visualization. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The concept of the distance measure is relevant in the context of welded knots, which are defined with respect to the cross-link planar representation of knots. The study also includes an examination of the distance measure's properties, as well as its relationships with other measures, such as the welded crossing number and the number of pass moves required to transform a knot diagram into a trivial unknot. We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we derive our cocycle, I(X), through the use of graph-based configuration space integrals rather than combinatorial approaches used by Mortier. This along with establishing a direct connection between the cocycle and the Casson invariant allows us to determine the order of its image under [X] to be order three rather than the order two determined by Mortier for his related cocycle. The name 'Gramain' is used to honor the memory of Paul Rainville, who in turn honored the memory of Jean Gramain. New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider sterile neutrinos, establishing a minimum mass for a single such neutrino flavour. The resulting constraints would likely be firmly established by the mid-2020s, thereby ensuring that any missing mass component around 0.5 eV/c^2 is explicitly identified. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Through our experiments, we learned that the breach's magnitude depends on the FL algorithm, whereas the attack's simplicity depends more on the user in question. Consequently, companies are advised to adopt a cautious, case-by-case approach when collaborating with other entities, potentially incorporating privacy-enhancing technologies to safeguard their data. Despite its restrictions, a reverse multiplication attack can still result in successful model recovery in certain situations, namely when the base model is trained using a single sample. Interestingly, even though a reverse sum attack can be executed with encrypted data, it cannot be carried out with data encryption methods that obfuscate the sum, thereby suggesting that those techniques can prevent the attack. Given that both attacks are feasible and successful, giving rise to potential privacy breaches, it is essential to investigate ways to enhance protocols' security, underscoring the significance of publicizing vulnerable FL implementations, as well as sharing techniques used by companies to defend against such breaches. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. The code has been made publicly available to facilitate further research. Additionally, the theoretical analysis and empirical findings facilitate a deeper understanding of the detection task and can serve as a foundation for more innovative research in this domain. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Our study shows that this self-balancing feature yields a substantial enhancement in gate reliability, especially for long chains, and our Molmer-Sorensen gate design exhibits lower failure rates compared to other gate techniques, particularly for intermediate-frequency errors. A simulation of this gate followed by a motivated logical operation shows that it can achieve an average fidelity of over 0.99 across frequencies ranging from -5 to 5 kilohertz for chains of two to thirty-three ions. This research offers a molecular-scale quantum computation technique offering greater frequency tolerance, an essential capability for the efficient operation of large-scale quantum systems.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of more accurate, detailed models that capture the underlying structure of the material. From these, we identified the smallest models that are stable and consistent with experimental data; two of these models can also be applied to similar materials. These discoveries open up possibilities for using computational modeling to design more effective materials. Additionally, we've determined that certain characteristics in barium titanate, such as the movement of certain atoms and the vibration of the molecular structure, can be controlled through changes to the volume of the material, and further that these changes are influenced by the presence of certain other atoms. Finally, we've established that computational modeling can accurately predict certain properties of barium titanate when it's in a different, polarized state.

In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer. A mathematical derivation, taking into account the gyroscope's rotation and the geometry of the Sagnac setup, yields an expression for the spectral shift, which is directly proportional to the rotation rate and angular momentum of the gyroscope. Experimental validation of this theory was conducted using a laser-based spectral analysis technique, demonstrating a linear relationship between the spectral shift and the gyroscope's rotation rate. This phenomenon is observable over a specific wavelength range, defined by the Sagnac interferometer's optical properties, and provides a direct means of measuring a gyroscope's angular momentum. Experimental measurements demonstrated a linear response to rotation rates up to 300 deg/s, with a proportionality constant of approximately 0.25 nm/s/deg. The gyroscope's angular momentum could be accurately determined using this method, with an uncertainty of less than 5%. The technique offers a highly sensitive, direct method for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum. The phenomenon of spectral shift around anomalies in a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer provides valuable insights into the interaction between high-finesse optical cavities and gyroscope systems, offering potential applications in the development of more precise gyroscope calibration methods. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack. Additionally, we have proposed the concept of a smart sensor that could provide an alternative solution to address this vulnerability. Our research highlights the importance of conducting in-depth security evaluations of complex systems, as well as the need to prioritize the security of systems that handle critical public safety components. Our unique approach to identifying this vulnerability and testing the attack and proposed solution in a real-world setting contribute new insights to the field of security research. Our study has the potential to spark further exploration of this type of attack and its applications. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. As a result, there is an urgent need for further research in this area, involving the development of methods to model storage units' risk behavior and assess their risk preferences. This knowledge could be used to enhance the effectiveness of pricing mechanisms and market participation strategies for storage units, ultimately allowing them to fully utilize their potential to stabilize the grid. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections, particularly for higher data transfer rates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings. The ACN protocol's superiority can be achieved by adapting the ACN parameters to optimize performance or by utilizing ACN in combination with other communication systems. The proposed ACN protocol offers a viable solution for next-generation VC systems and has the potential to be effectively implemented with current mobility management techniques. Additionally, our research provides a theoretical framework and practical recommendations for the ACN protocol's effective deployment. Lastly, we outline potential paths for future research in this area.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, an increase in frequency bandwidth and density of cells leads to better optimization under these conditions. This approach also offers greater flexibility than static TDD in terms of performance.

This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that vacancy activation energies are significantly lower than those of isolated vortex lines, offering a framework that could potentially inform and guide other research in this area. Moreover, our findings emphasize the importance of accounting for vortex correlations when analyzing the vortex state and, more broadly, underpin the necessity of considering many-body effects in the study of strongly interacting vortex systems. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems. These charactersizations facilitate the identification of sufficient conditions for ground states in 2-dimensional systems with matrix product operator dynamics. We demonstrate this concept through examples involving both fractional and integral symmetries. Our study also reveals the role of commutant squares in relation to bimodules and the category of Morita, thereby offering a category theoretical description of 4-tensors resulting from commutant squares. This approach is seen to provide the basis for a generalization of the Haagerup approximation theorem. We then establish the existence of an approximation of commutant squares using matrix units from partially ordered abelian subalgebras, and this characterization enables us to introduce a new tensor norm for commutant squares. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Additionally, we applied the system to one real-world dataset and observed significant improvements in reliability and a modest improvement in accuracy for another dataset. Furthermore, we conducted experiments utilizing human trust labels and found that the system's reliability metric correlates strongly with these labels. The proposed system is available open-source under the MIT license at the following repository: https://github.com/huggingface/diffusion-safety-net. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AJROcean/HiXray.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we discover $J_n^T$ can be defined through a virtual biperiodic link, and provide computational data suggesting it may behave interestingly for non-trivial biperiodic links. This framework is also applicable to knots, and we propose calling the knot version of this polynomial the colored knot Jones polynomial, denoted as $J_n^K$. Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  The studies demonstrate rigorous reliability with both monosemous and polysemous word evaluations, along with an assessment of the consistency of best model performance across iterations.  The proposed method achieves top-ranked scores in three independent evaluation datasets, showcasing its capacity for good performance in a range of domain settings. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, top quark single-production cross-section measurements were made, and the data was found to align with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Top quark pair events were used to develop new methods to correct for detection biases and estimate uncertainty, along with top quark single-production events used to test the sensitivity of these methods. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of top quark pair and single-production processes in proton-lead collisions at 8.16 TeV, and can serve as a reference for future studies at higher center-of-mass energies. The presented methods to correct for detection biases in top quark pair and single-production events can be applied to other sensitive searches in particle physics experiments. The publicly available tool THNNTop was used for these analyses to help develop event selection criteria, estimate cross-sections, and correct for detection biases. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. We build a modern, versatile dataset called CMS (Music Captioning Dataset) consisting of 5,000 captioned playlists, which serves as both a dataset for captioning and retrieval tasks. Each captioned playlist contains a brief description, such as the title provided by the original creator or a suggested alternative, which provides both a starting point and a benchmark for assessment. We also establish a set of evaluation metrics that account for both factual accuracy and descriptive quality. Furthermore, we designate a suitable model architecture for music captioning, which can be trained using a limited number of training examples, which is a characteristic essential for a practical music captioning solution. We conducted experiments using our proposed model and guidelines for captioning best practices, which yielded promising results on the CMS dataset. The evaluations revealed that our proposed approach performs well above baseline methods and is capable of handling the high linguistic variability observed within music captions. Nonetheless, there remains significant room for improvement and further research within this newly introduced music captioning domain. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. This new stochastic hydrodynamic approach provides a flexible tool for studying interacting Bose gases, and can be used in conjunction with experimental observations of quantum shocks in Bose-Einstein condensates. Additionally, it encompasses the Bogoliubov approach as a subset, and is conducive to further development of related theories. This approach can also be paired with microscopic simulations, and offers a hydrodynamic perspective on the underlying physics involved. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. This theory offers a unifying explanation for the distinctities observed between inner and outer modes, where the presence of an outer mode is seen as simply an inner mode occurring after a two-ELM event. This new perspective also prompts the question of whether an inner mode could arise from the capture of 'holes' on a q=4 surface, a hypothesis yet to be tested. Ultimately, this study provides a fresh insight that may contribute to the long-sought understanding of palm tree modes. It also highlights the importance of investigating the relationships between core plasma and the edge/local magnetic field, as well as the interaction between edge plasma and turbulence. Lastly, it emphasizes the value of combining observational analysis with computer modeling to gain a deeper understanding of such complex magnetic phenomena. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our research indicates that the complex baseband output of the radar system, influenced by the IRS, follows a non-central chi-square distribution, enabling us to derive the probability density function (PDF) for a special case where the LOS and NLOS links have equal strengths. Based on these findings, we propose suboptimal yet efficient algorithms for target parameter estimation, including the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) and the Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimator, and provide corresponding performance comparisons. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms in scenarios where the IRS-provided virtual link has similar strength to the LOS link. Additionally, we investigate the efficacy of these algorithms in scenarios where the LOS link has weaker strength than the NLOS link, and discuss the implications of using the ML estimator in such cases. Finally, we discuss the potential applications and future research directions for this concept, especially in multi-target scenarios and with multiple IRS nodes. The proposed method provides a theoretical foundation for using IRS technology in radar systems, and the findings presented can serve as a starting point for further research into target parameter estimation in such systems. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. The proposed evaluation framework has been made publicly accessible to facilitate the comparative evaluation of new fuzzers. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. To further validate our proposal, we also analyzed the NMC's performance on the CoRe 50 benchmark and explored its extensions, including the use of multiple class prototypes and boundary adjustment. Our findings have significant implications for the study of continual learning, suggesting that the advancements seen in state-of-the-art models can be attributed more to the models' ability to generalize across classes rather than the complex mechanisms employed.
