Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our study shows that in such scenarios, using j=10-fold CV outperforms the standard 5-fold CV method across all datasets examined, outperforming the standard method by an average of 0.9% and as much as 5.5%. Moreover, as model size increases, our proposed method proves particularly effective in achieving better performance. In particular, our study reveals that for large models, using j=10-fold CV reduces the threat of overfitting, as confirmed by both accuracy and threat metrics. Our research's findings are made accessible to the community via an open repository allowing the reproduction of obtained results. Moreover, both model performance and code are made freely available to facilitate further research within this domain. In conclusion, our study's findings underscore the importance of mitigating performance estimation's variance when conducting parameter tuning, as is demonstrated by the consistent superiority of j=10-fold CV over 5-fold CV across all tested datasets. Consequently, in accordance with our proposed method's aims, computational resources should be allocated to reduce variance, rather than bias, and our study provides the community with tangible evidence supporting this approach. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, whereas in ultracold atomic systems,
the required mechanism involves the pair hopping process. Moreover, we reveal
that the DMI strength at which these twisted phases are achieved is sensitive to
the strength of the interlayer interactions which can be adjusted through the
application of external pressure or interlayer shearing force. Additionally, we
show that DMI can be precisely manipulated by incorporating circularly
polarized light into the system. Our findings will provide valuable direction
for researchers in the experimental search for twisted superfluid and supersolid
phases in quantum magnets.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Furthermore, this approach enables the simple determination of reconstruction parameters, thereby minimizing trial and error in 4D MRI image construction. Additionally, a publicly accessible software package has been developed for the motion-compensated rCASPR algorithm, making it easily implementable for the continuous, free-breathing MRI sequence. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, the combinatorial structure of the loom space can be reflected in a graph structure associated with the triangulation, and this graph's 4-colorability can be determined by analyzing the loom space's properties. In cases where this graph is 4-colorable, it is possible to label its nodes with colors that correspond to vertex orientations in the triangulation. Ultimately, this labeling can inform the construction of a pseudo-Anosov flow whose link space is topologically equivalent to the loom space, thus establishing a significant connection between the theories of veering triangulations and pseudo-Anosov flows. Additionally, this relationship is utilized to prove that the graph associated with a loom space always has a highly non-trivial 4-colorability property known as "recognizable". The notion of recognizable 4-colorability is then further expanded to encompass a broader concept called "strongly recognizable', which applies to the graph structure of a specific type of loom space called 'orbit looms'. These new properties of loom spaces provide key insights into the combinatorial structure of veering triangulations and their associated graph structures. Lastly, notable examples of loom spaces with strongly recognizable 4-colorability are introduced, alongside a discussion of additional properties and potential directions for further research. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. In addition, Kedge's edge sparsification pattern reveals insightful mechanisms of graph signal propagation and facilitates the interpretation of model predictions. With Kedge, users can develop a deeper understanding of model decisions by visualizing the reduced graph structure along with the identified neighbor nodes. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets and models validate Kedge's effectiveness, and the code is openly available for community use. Overall, Kedge introduces a significant innovation in graph sparsification, and its effective reduction of graph edges has far-reaching implications for the study and application of GNNs. As a result, Kedge is an essential technique for enhancing the interpretability of GNN models. In addition to facilitating the understanding of model decisions, Kedge may also contribute to decreased memory usage and computational costs during both training and inference. In this paper, we introduce Kedge in a general form that is applicable to a wide range of graph-based deep learning models, and we provide specific implementations of Kedge for graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, and GNNs combining both techniques. Moreover, we explore various distributional variants of Kedge, and we discuss open challenges and possible research directions in the field of graph sparsification and adaptation. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this study introduces a new feedback-efficient sketch called the $F^2$ sketch, which employs a strategy called the classic estimator with a familiar component and a novel component with a unique attribute, and this estimator exhibits an outstanding performance when dealing with vectors that have only slight changes since the sketch was created, a scenario that arises frequently in the context of streaming algorithms. The $F^2$ sketch offers an exceptionally efficient estimator that, with the assistance of just a limited number of queries per vector, can accurately determine the top elements of previous vectors, which is a crucial advantage. To further illustrate the value of this new sketch, we demonstrate its utility in enhancing the performance of the well-known median-finding problem and the top elements of Euclidean norms, both of which have been examined extensively. The $F^2$ sketch can be considered a crucial tool that can enhance the functionality of various streaming algorithms in various applications by equipping them with a powerful dimensionality reduction technique that is both efficient and robust. A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that induces a thermal gradient. This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our simulations indicate that CLIC has better sensitivity to the mass dimension effective operators, whereas ILC is more sensitive to the global normalization parameter in the HEFT and to the top quadratic coefficient in the SMEFT. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrates that double Higgs production at these colliders can provide significant insights into the properties of the Higgs boson and the underlying new physics governing the Higgs sector.

The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Additionally, we observed evidence suggesting that outflows can supply gas to necessary regions for star formation, such as molecular clouds, through the process of gas re-circulation. This process may help maintain the necessary fuel for ongoing star formation over the galaxy's history. As a result, outflows could play a key role in governing the galaxy's gas usage and conversion of gas into stars, influencing how the galaxy develops over time. Lastly, we noticed that outflows are directed almost perpendicular to the plane of the galaxy, a characteristic also seen in more normal galaxies, and suggested that this outflow orientation may be a consequence of how gas is pulled into massive stars and subjected to outflows. Further research is needed to validate these findings and outflow characteristics in various types of galaxies. Our study provides new insights into the physical processes governing the interaction between outflows and star formation within a distant starburst galaxy. As a result, this study can inform computational models of galaxy evolution, which often disregard outflows due to their complex nature, by incorporating them as a crucial element that affects how gas is converted into stars. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. As a result, BoAnon is an highly effective BO framework for auto-tuning computer systems. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. Additionally, it discusses developments in neutral B-meson mixing, particularly the detection of overlying collisions in high-multiplicity LHC experiments and techniques used to mitigate their influence. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach enables the development of more accurate simulation tools capable of efficiently training deep learning models for self-driving vehicles. With SceneGen, we achieve superior performance when compared to existing traffic scenario models, according to metrics such as mean absolute error and Kullback-Leibler divergence. Additionally, we incorporate SceneGen into a unified framework that integrates both density estimation and rendering components, ultimately resulting in a highly optimized traffic scenario model. Through the modification of SceneGen's density estimation component, we successfully extend the model's applicability to generate scenarios in cities beyond those used in the training dataset. Ultimately, this advancement enables the efficient transfer of learned scenes to new cities through a process involving just a single example per target city. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. The code for our research is available at https://github.com/yunsong-ai/farfus. It includes the fusion algorithm for detecting far-field objects, which achieved top scores on the newly-created benchmark datasets. We've also open-sourced the protocol and the dataset, hoping it will inspire further innovation in this important area for autonomous vehicles. Keywords: Far-Field 3D Detection, Autonomous Driving, 3D Detection Benchmark, Fusion Algorithm, Object Detection. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This implies that the parameters of the papillon graph, which are relatively short, completely characterize its structure. We conclude by determining the papillon graph with the smallest possible number of vertices. This represents a significant breakthrough, as it answers a question posed by the first author in 1991. The papillon graph will enable us to solve another problem, posed by Chellada and So in 1975, regarding the smallest number of vertices in a cubic graph with the PMH-property. This will result in a new lower bound for this class of graphs. Finally, we will use the papillon graph to solve a further question posed by the first author in 1991, regarding the smallest number of vertices in a cubic graph with the E2F condition, as well as determine the smallest number of vertices in a cubic graph with the PMH-property. The papillon graph will enable us to set a new lower bound for both these classes of graphs. The name 'papillon' is derived from the French word for butterfly, as the graph's structure resembles a pair of wings that are integrated in a cubic graph. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe Timeloops could serve as a model for developing system call learning techniques applicable to a broader range of programs. The Timeloops project is currently available under the permissive MIT license on GitHub. Moreover, we have published a small-scale experimental study showing the system call learning capabilities of Timeloops. This experiment involved both a solo run and a concurrent test involving two separate services, along with the system events generated by these services. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Additionally, an optimal control problem is formulated and shown to possess a minimized solution, which can be characterized through the combination of a state and adjoint system. Furthermore, our analysis involves comparing the optimal control to a singular optimal control, obtained through the application of a transversality condition, resulting in a unique minimizer for the singular optimal control problem. This analytical framework is set against the backdrop of recent studies on similar population control models. Notably, in those works, controls were allowed in the nonlinear diffusion component only, whereas our work investigates the additional challenge of controlling the population dynamics in the presence of an interior degenerate diffusion with nonlinear boundary feedback. This research is an extension of the author's PhD thesis, which provided the foundational analysis for the main results presented here. However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data suggests that IGR J19294+1816 exhibits significant variability in its spectral characteristics and light curve, ultimately showcasing the need for continuous observational monitoring of this intriguing phenomenon. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our study reveals that the performance of these 
designs holds up to electron speeds of 300 kiloelectrons/volt. We also explore the 
limitations of this method's effectiveness and provide design guidelines for such 
phase plates in relation to the electron probe and its relationship to the TEM's 
acceleration voltage. Lastly, we demonstrate the feasibility of these designs 
throughout actual TEM experiments. Our research demonstrates the capability of 
programmable phase plates to attain extremely high-resolution images, with results 
highlighting the vast potential of this aberration-correcting technique.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations, rather than generative capabilities, are the distinguishing factor in these evaluations. Additionally, an analysis of the influence of evaluation tasks, models, and datasets revealed that the underlying characteristics of these datasets play a significant role in this outcome. In conclusion, this work emphasizes the importance of examining dialogue model encoder representations to ensure they align with expected preferences and norms of dialogue Interactions. Moreover, it paves the way for further research aimed at enhancing the underlying understanding of these encoder representations. The code and data used in this work are available for public access at https://github.com/ghrua/Eval-Dialog-Encoders.

To tackle this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections. Nonetheless, this model remains prone to ring-loss cases due to a lack of explicit loop-closure guidance, resulting in loop-closure context being incorporated at the expense of contextual modulation. Consequently, a more dependable loop-closure model is proposed to address this challenge. The proposed approach demonstrates improved loop-closure ability and is deemed a viable foundation for autonomous systems operating in complex, indoor scenarios. The study also highlights the challenge of developing a LiDAR-based place recognition model capable of performing pure loop closures in complex environments. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The velocity of charge carriers can be extracted from the thermal capacity measurements, albeit requiring extremely low temperatures. At finite temperatures, however, the thermal capacity is dominated by thermal screening and we have developed a simplified theoretical approach to predict it through interaction-strength-independent formulas, which are specific to the underlying lattice structure. We have validated our results for thermodynamic properties against accurate numerical simulations. We also demonstrate that the compressibility of doped graphene exhibits a universal temperature dependence governed by the velocity of charge carriers, with an explicit numerical value that can be derived from thermal capacity measurements. The universal temperature-dependent term in the compressibility is however only observable at very low temperatures. At finite temperatures, the compressibility is dominated by thermal screening and we have established a universal relationship to predict it through the interaction strength and the lattice structure. These findings provide a universal framework for understanding the thermal screening and thermal properties of doped graphene, regardless of the specific method used to populate the Dirac bands. We have also identified the criteria for using simple lattice-strength-only formulas to predict thermal capacity and compressibility in finite-width nanostructures of dirac materials. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Our findings suggest that context-aware acoustic feature engineering plays a crucial role in speech synthesis. Moreover, by incorporating contextual semantic elements, fine-grained speech patterns can be produced with greater ease. We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis also enables us to draw conclusions about the module properties of the base field Q itself when given certain highly ramified polynomials, leading to an extension of a prior result by Bushnell and Haines. Additionally, we establish a closer relationship between the module properties of such a given highly ramified polynomial and a new, specifically constructed polynomial that is obtained by applying a certain automorphism to the Galois group associated with the original polynomial. This relationship, though locally equivalent to a simple permutation action, still exhibits a more complex behaviour when considered in a global context. The developed techniques are further used to investigate various properties of a new, infinitely ramified Q(G_s)-algebra, which is obtained by applying a certain automorphism to the rational Q(G_s)-algebra, for a suitably chosen arithmetic group G_s. Furthermore, we establish a new description of the ring of integers in a specific, infinitely ramified Q(algebraic closure of Q(_p)) extension, and show that this description leads to a free module over the associated order within the rational Q(G_s)-algebra, for a particular prism field Q(_p). This conclusion, though it already follows directly from the mentioned earlier results by Bushnell and Haines, still provides a useful new proof. Finally, we derive additional conclusions about the additive Galois module properties of certain infinitely ramified Q(algebraic closure of Q(_p)) extensions, and present open questions in this field.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. We also introduce BART-DSC, a contextualized diachronic semantic
change detector, with data and models available at https://github.com/
hahnfran/BART-DSC. We hope this research will help move context-based
studies ahead. We appreciate the behind-the-scenes support from Google
Research, and the contextual contributions from Jason Bailey and Christopher
Manning. We also thank the anonymous reviewers and Christopher Potts for their

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we establish upper limits on the decay constant of ketoaxions, determining that their decay constant must be less than $10^{-22}$ times the corresponding value for axions. This research thus fills the gap in parameter space left by experiments such as the one conducted at the Hubble Space Telescope and sets new limits on the properties of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles. This research provides a framework for the investigation of black holes in AGNs and offers a powerful tool for confronting theories of General Relativity in high-energy environments. This research can be extended to other sources of gravitational waves and offers a novel perspective on the relationship between the properties of black holes and their surroundings. This research paves the way for the analysis of spatial surveys of gravitational waves, allowing for the investigation of the properties of black holes and the physics of gravitational wave emission. This research can also be applied to studying black hole mergers, such as GW150914, providing new perspectives on the relationship between the merging binaries and their environment. This research thus marks the beginning of a new line of investigation, one that will require a more in-depth, sophisticated model of black hole formation and a deeper understanding of how the properties of black holes are linked to their surroundings

the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we propose that retinal IKNM could

will give rise to an emergent length scale on the order of 10 to 100 $e^2$

liquids.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, we recorded a neutron detection rate of around 50 per day, and measured the spectrum of super-neutrinofiltered neutrons. Furthermore, we collected data with both the super-neutrinofilter in place and removed, to calculate a sensitivity of the method and evaluate its capability to study the dependence of spallation neutron yields on muon energy. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications of this design to similar laboratory setups located within deep laboratories around the world.

Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  To verify accounts, a similar approach was applied but with additional steps including the extraction of date of birth, place of birth, and ID number which resulted in an F-score of 0.73 when tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images.  This indicates that the system can effectively convert ID cards into readable text, making it an efficient method for verifying accounts.  The proposed system was compared to an existing service that converts IDs into text format, demonstrating its higher accuracy. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, they provide a foundation for exploring the biological mechanisms underlying the animacy principle and its connections to other visual categorization systems in VTC. Ultimately, this work encourages the development of more comprehensive theoretical models of VTC's organization and the multi-faceted nature of animacy within it.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. However, our analysis suggests that even a very small transmission of the virus during that single event could have a negligible impact if rigorous preventive measures are observed, which is compatible with recent analyses of the COVID-19 pandemic. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through a series of Monte Carlo simulations of Gaussian ensemble, specifically in tackling the sign problem at various filling levels, and by applying it to the study of fermion-dimer systems, which typically face a severe sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings reveal that the phase structures obtained through this method closely resemble those derived from exact umbrella sampling or centered shifted score estimators, further highlighting the general applicability and effectiveness of our architecture. The technical simplicity and computational efficiency of our method make it an attractive solution for any Monte Carlo sign problem that can be differentiable. The source code for our method is openly available online. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. Existing research studies on this topic have been comprehensively examined.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be found at the address indicated in the paper. The paper's findings demonstrate the capability of efficient hyperparameter tuning to result in substantial improvements in private deep learning models' performance.

The study involved using a two-component model to break down elemental patterns into supernovae types and then comparing observed values to predicted values. The findings revealed similar elemental patterns in outer regions of the galaxy, variations in satellite galaxies and star clusters like omega Centauri, and differences in abundance of elements in outer regions compared to inner regions. The study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the formation and chemical evolution of the galaxy. It also highlights the need for additional data to clarify variations in star compositions and the processes that shape elemental patterns. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our findings provide valuable insights into the propagation mechanics of online rumors and may contribute to the development of more effective counter-measures. Furthermore, the data collected can be utilized for other applications involving social media platforms. Additionally, our methodology may be expanded to address other issues arising from the spread of information. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. Moreover, a significant dispersion was observed in the frequencies of planetary nebulae within individual galaxies, and a notable positive correlation was observed between these frequencies and the galaxies' overall mass, indicating that the detection of planetary nebulae is significantly influenced by mass density within these galaxies. By comparing the observed frequencies of planetary nebulae within individual galaxies to predicted values under uniform brightness conditions, a notable spread was observed, and a notable variation was observed in the distribution styles of planetary nebulae within different galaxies, and a notable correlation was observed between these distributions and the galaxies' overall mass, indicating that mass density has a significant influence on the formation and evolution of planetary nebulae within these galaxies. A statistical analysis of the velocities of planetary nebulae within these galaxies revealed a significant spread and a correlation with galaxies' overall mass, indicating a relationship between the masses of planetary nebulae and the galaxies within which they reside. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream's capability to execute queries efficiently, even with limited knowledge of performance-critical details, makes it an excellent choice for application developers who need to optimize database queries quickly. To showcase LifeStream's effectiveness in real-world scenarios, we successfully applied it to enhance the accuracy of clinical diagnoses. In particular, we employed LifeStream to implement leading medical research algorithms, achieving notable improvements and demonstrating the potential for LifeStream to drive significant advancements in healthcare informatics. By combining efficient computation, a lightweight in-memory architecture, and simple-to-use SQL extensions with outstanding performance, LifeStream provides a superior data processing solution, especially tailored for flexible and fast healthcare data analysis. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. The definition of the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve is shown to be equivalent to a curve whose binormal vector is constant and negative in the cross product with the vector that maps to the previous curve, under a specific transformation. In addition, the classification of open, closed, and periodic curves is extended to a higher dimensional space and the distinction between them is clarified. It is also proven that a curve does not repeat itself and is not completely straight if it is both a Bertrand and a Chaprat curve in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To further explore this concept, we conducted experiments using both the KL divergence and another novel loss function, both yielding unexpected results. Our findings indicate that, counter to intuitive expectations, these loss functions can lead to accurate classification outcomes, despite being designed to minimize discrepancy between probability distributions, rather than being tailored to loss specifications. To gain deeper insight, we developed a mathematical analysis to differentiate the losses we tested from the neural network's dynamic parameters, building on existing work. Our research offers a comprehensive investigation of loss functions in the context of neural network classification, facilitating enhanced understanding of loss function selection. Additionally, our novel loss functions can serve as a starting point for further research and optimization in this area. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. The objective of this control strategy is to eliminate a destabilizing surface force by controlling the flow at one boundary, specifically the upper boundary in a two-dimensional periodic domain. Ultimately, this design framework can be applied to other fluid dynamics models, such as the Klemond-Biot equations, by recognizing the Navier-Stokes equations as a particular case with specific permeability properties. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. The ability of the model to predict material behavior in different experimental setups is demonstrated through the simulation of large cyclic deformations with strain-induced crystallization. The theoretical model and numerical method are validated against experimental data obtained using micro-CT and thermal analysis techniques as well as other existing models. The proposed approach offers a comprehensive framework for modeling strain-induced crystallization in polymer materials. However, further research is needed to address model parameter identification challenges. The proposed model and associated numerical method demonstrate effective prediction of material structure and temperature evolution during large cyclic deformations, which can occur in various applications of flexible polymers subject to repeated loading. Hence, this model has significant implications for the development of polymer materials and their applications. To this end, the model should be combined with kinetic modeling of crystallization to explore its broader implications. Additionally, model parameters can be identified through comparison with additional experimental data, including studies of crystallization kinetics. Ultimately, this model has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of polymer materials, which will involve significant further research and experimentation. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Despite the computational nature of these findings, they hold significant theoretical importance. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our findings show that our method can effectively learn to prefer optimal feedback by itself, leading to a notable improvement in its ability to generalize across different forms of noisy feedback. Furthermore, we can achieve comparable performance to algorithms designed specifically for different forms of noisy feedback, thus showcasing the versatility of our approach. Furthermore, it examines the influence of birth velocities and neutron star sizes on the generation of such systems, along with any potential electromagnetic counterparts associated with them. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  The model's code is available for use at https://github.com/zyang01/DISR.  The paper's findings prove that a integrated real rain simulation and elimination model is feasible and efficient at removing rain from images.
