A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. Moreover, we establish that continuous control Lyapunov functions can be replaced by their continuous counterparts in certain situations. Lastly, we outline conditions under which the relationships between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions apply to the impulsive systems resulting from bounded open-loop controls. These connections facilitate the stabilization of periodic orbits and the resolution of the multi-target problem without relying on time-dependent controls. Notably, this research is accompanied by computationally verifiable criteria based on control Lyapunov functions, which can be determined through standard optimization methods. In the case of polynomial control systems, these criteria become specifically feasible algorithms. Lastly, this research is highlighted by an example involving a system of differential equations that models competition among species in an ecological environment. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, EBOS introduces an innovative technique for visualizing the uncertainty dimension, and delivers impressive performance in unsupervised uncertainty modeling. Evaluations across multiple datasets reveal substantial gains in confidence calibration, with performance improvements of $10.9\pm0.8\%$ and $25.3\pm2.5\%$ when compared to state-of-the-art baselines using single-network and multi-network settings, respectively. Moreover, EBOS exhibits superior performance in unsupervised uncertainty modeling tasks, such as uncertainty discrimination and semi-supervised learning. Our findings highlight the superiority of Energy-based Open-World Softmax for both supervised confidence calibration and unsupervised uncertainty modeling. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw/EBOS.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The code and environment are available online at https://github.com/Mistral42/L2Explorer, and we invite the research community to join us in exploring this groundbreaking benchmark environment. The L2Explorer website is also accessible at https://l2explorer.github.io/. The L2Explorer framework is part of the DeepSafe benchmark suite, a comprehensive collection of challenging evaluation scenarios for lifelong learning methods. The suite is designed to facilitate open competition among researchers worldwide, focusing on advancing the capabilities of safe, continuous learning models through rigorous assessment and rigorous testing in realistic, simulated environments. The winning entries will be featured in a high-level review presenting the top-performing methods, along with corresponding code, and highlighting the achievements of the top-ranking teams. The L2Explorer framework is an important contribution to the development of lasting evaluation methods, and we anticipate that this benchmark environment, along with our evaluation framework and methodology, will play a key role in shaping the future direction of research in continual learning. In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that higher-order approximations are necessary to analyze wave propagation in one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, unlike in two-dimensional quasicrystals which can be analyzed using first-order approximations. This study provides significant insights into the dynamics of wave propagation in one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures and suggests new paths for developing non-localized waves in one-dimensional systems. Furthermore, our findings may contribute to the development of new techniques for determining dimerized interactions in physical systems, particularly through the application of optical manipulation. This study is a crucial step in expanding our understanding of wave propagation in quasiperiodic structures, extending beyond the limits of localization and non-localization in one-dimensional systems, and may pave the way for the development of new wave propagation phenomena in one-dimensional systems. Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory. In operation, the Data Reduction System will receive raw data from the telescope's control system, apply various data processing steps, and transmit the output to the scientists and the archive. We have successfully demonstrated the functionality of this prototype and are currently integrating it with the observatory's software systems. Once integrated, we plan to operate the Data Reduction System in a simulated environment to prepare for its eventual integration with the all-sky adaptive-optics system and the Keck System Automation. This prototype marks a significant step in the development of Liger's data processing and underscores the importance of this customized solution in delivering the full potential of Liger and the Keck Observatory. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Our study therefore enables the realization of optimal SPADE protocols that realize super-resolution in scenarios where standard techniques fall short. Moreover, we illustrate the feasibility of this approach using a specific example where the projection of both photons onto lateral Hermite-Gauss modes allows for the demonstration of super-resolution in a particular experiment. Our work therefore enables the optimal realization of SPADE protocols that facilitate the optimal use of quantum correlations to achieve the highest possible resolution in optical super-resolution. In doing so, we provide a framework for optimizing SPADE that can be applied to any type of entangled source. Additionally, we show that our approach can be robust to errors in the characterization of the entangled source and the SPADE protocol, and can be used to develop super-resolution SPADE protocols that are optimal in the absence of errors. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. The principles developed in this research can be applied to other singularly perturbed systems with similar Hopf bifurcations. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This implies a fundamental connection between the construction of massive galaxies and the shape of the mass-star formation rate relation. Models such as Horizon-AGN and Gong have already incorporated interactions between bulge growth and star formation rate slope. As a result of these findings, further refinements to these models may be necessary to accurately replicate this critical mass transition point. Alongside analyzing the main sequence of galaxies, this study also explores the relationship between bulge formation and galaxy morphology. As expected, a stronger relationship exists between the index $n$ and construction of massive bulges rather than the bulge-to-total mass ratio itself. Therefore, the density of central mass within galaxies serves as a better predictor of star formation within bulges. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The evaluation shows that, subject to precise fence cost models, our method's performance is comparable to existing solutions handling single fence cost models. In cases where cost models vary, our approach's performance remains relatively stable, albeit with some variability. Overall, the results validate the correctness of our method across different fence costs and examples, safety criteria, and fence types. Moreover, the performance gains derived from optimal fence placement outperform existing single-fence based methods by an average of 1.37-fold. Furthermore, concrete examples illustrate the applicability of our method to various programs and program components. The counter-example driven fence insertion procedure's feasibility is also confirmed through protocol verification cases. Finally, our method's scalability is demonstrated across a range of program safety criteria validations. The formal framework, algorithm descriptions, prototype code, benchmark data, and additional examples are available at the associated repository. The counter-example driven fence insertion procedure has the potential to optimize multiple fence types, offering a relatively stable performance outcome despite the complexities involved. The results show that our method correctly validates program safety criteria and places fences more efficiently than existing methods. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. This outcome is confirmed through calculations of the classical driver force and Lyapunov exponent. Additionally, we demonstrate that the introduction of a harmonic oscillator's quantum oscillator strength can transition the system from a chaotic to a stable state. Our findings provide tangible evidence for the role of quantum effects in generating chaotic states in stable classical systems. Moreover, we propose that this quantum chaos mechanism could be a universal phenomenon applicable across various classical driving forces. As an aside, we highlight the utility of our variational approach in facilitating the comparison of quantum and classical dynamics for this H\'enon-Heiles system. This involves showing that the total angular momentum exhibits a diagonalized structure similar to that observed in classical mechanics. This work is further bolstered by four accompanying figures that illustrate the evolution of the H\'enon-Heiles system under influence of classical driving forces, as well as the effects of introducing a harmonic oscillator's quantum oscillator strength. The study is also supported by two accompanying movies that visually display the behavior of the system in both the absence and presence of quantum oscillator strength. If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Furthermore, this factorization of W into a monadic structure and a natural transformation from that structure to itself reveals a connection to the Kleiman-Bousfield functor structure. This paper develops the simplicial universal bundle functor W further, giving it in terms of a natural transformation of functors that arise from the monadic structure, and then uses this expression to show a related result about the simplicial Dold-Kan correspondence. Finally, this approach is applied to achieve a more direct proof of a related result to that of H. P. Russell. Russell's result concerns the effect of applying the simplicial Dold-Kan correspondence twice, and it does this by analyzing the identity map on the simplicial category in a certain abelian category of simplicial abelian groups. This line of reasoning is replaced by one based on the monic and epic structures within the simplicial category, and these for group theory were previously established by to be equivalent to the classical universal bundle functor W and its inverse, respectively. Therefore, this line of reasoning results in an even more direct proof of Russell's result than before. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zeangit/Sabra-vrd. Our work provides an effective solution to the VRD false positive issue and offers actionable insights for future research. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The performance capabilities of the CAPP were further assessed by executing various search algorithms, including hash tables, sorted lists, and binary search, which showed the CAPP to be comparable to a high-speed CPU like the Intel Core i7-6700K. The integration of multiple CAPPs was also explored, showcasing how multiple content-addressable arrays could be combined to achieve greater performance and data capacity – a crucial feature for large-scale parallel processing applications. The CAPP's potential in various fields, including machine learning, network routing, and database management, is also discussed, and the associated source code and system descriptions are available online as an open-source project on GitHub. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero. These findings are achieved through the development of a new compactness criterion in the context of Strauss's conjecture. 

This research addresses a critical question initially proposed by Brezis and Nirenberg in their paper 'A Nonlinear Elliptic Equation For An Infinite Flat Plane', which also includes significant contributions to the broader topic of supercritical elliptic equations. The work presented here also establishes a key connection between the symmetry of Q(y) and the symmetry of the "bubbling solutions'. It's important to note that Q(y)'s local minimum cannot be greater than zero to obtain these results; if it is, "bubbling solutions' will not exist. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure. Furthermore, we observe our approach succeeds where the other strategies fail, delivering code up to 20 lines long compared to their limited capacity to generate longer sections of code. The code and data for this project is available at https://github.com/hjchai/CodeGenerationNS.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Studies of the November 7th, 2004 event offer new insights into solar particle radiation and its effects on Earth's surface. Furthermore, researchers were able to model the development of a secondary radiation wave observed in protons, suggesting that this secondary wave may have been caused by the dispersion of initial particles as their measurements included particles that had not yet reached their maximum energy and therefore were not fully accelerated. In addition, the model predicted that the primary radiation wave's absorption could be attributed to photon-electron scattering, resulting in a 16-minute delay between the solar flare and the onset of particle radiation, a gap that was in fact present but much more concise (around 5 minutes). Researchers also discovered that secondary protons, detected at higher altitudes, had a more pronounced wave pattern than those detected at lower altitudes. Lastly, this event provided a chance to apply a new method of radiation danger assessment, one based on the ability to anticipate the formation of secondary wave patterns in particles. If successful, this could enable prompt warnings to be issued to spacecraft and aircraft traveling through regions expected to be hit by solar flares. However, it would require significant improvements to prediction models of solar flare-toffect interactions. Additionally, it is also proposed that shallow neutron detections, found previously on board ISEE3 and terrestrially in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, may have originated from the decay of neutrons captured by atoms in deep space and on board satellites and on Earth's surface, a phenomenon that could provide a unique tool for studying the composition of deep space and its atomic content. Moreover, it is also suggested that a a deeper examination of these events, along with a re-evaluation of historical data, may provide significant insights into solar particle radiation and its effects on Earth's surface, as well as allow for the development of more effective danger assessment

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. Our study demonstrates that our quantum-inspired method not only achieves comparable performance to these methods but also adapts quickly to data shifts, surpassing them in shift-detection metrics and supporting our proposal of the algorithm as effective for stream data. The code is available at https://github.com/leodst/qmaan.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Conversely, we find that even the most recent case law cited in the paper does not necessitate a reevaluation of our conclusions about compelled decryption. Nevertheless, we believe that our framework, in addition to its theoretical value, can also provide a useful basis for evaluating specific cases involving compelled acts in cryptography. Lastly, we propose our framework as a potential tool to facilitate a broader discussion aimed at developing a more cohesive approach to addressing compelled actability issues in cryptography. This discussion, we hope, will contribute to a greater understanding of the complex relationship between cryptography, security, and civil liberties in the context of compelled acts of encryption or decryption. This paper is part of a larger research project examining the interplay between cryptography, security, and civil liberties in the context of compelled acts of encryption or decryption. This paper is an independent contribution that is not necessitated by the project's goals. Instead, it is an initiative taken to engage with the ideas presented in a paper published by Daniel J. Solove, titled 'If you know the passcode, you have the key: A theory of compelled decryption', which was published in the Harvard Law Review in 2002. That paper introduced a novel approach to interpreting the established legal doctrine set forth in the case of Fisher v. US, as well as a framework for identifying specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, an evaluation of the system's ability to recognize false information on new events revealed a remarkable 10% improvement in the F1-score. The MetaFEND system's capability to identify false information on new events without relying on additional training is a significant advancement in the field of false information detection. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This is in alignment with similar results seen in one-dimensional periodic Euler and Boussinesq equations. Notably, it is proven that the solution will develop a finite-scale blow-up within a critical time frame of $O(1)$ through the construction of a non-uniform bound, followed by the establishment of a non-uniform estimate for the solution's blow-up time using an approach inspired by the strategy used in similar scenarios. It is also shown that the formation of singularity is controlled and bounded by a universal dyadic bound, as proven through an approach involving the construction of a model equation and its analysis. It is also proven that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the optimal bound for the blow-up time can be estimated as $$
T^{*}-\epsilon\leq\frac{4}{\|u_{0,x}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}.
$$

$$

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Finally, we conduct numerical analyses to present results for M/M/1/1 and M/G/1/1 queues.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Furthermore, a short circuit method is presented to generate GCA in any desired dimension from existing lower-dimensional arrays. Finally, a few notable GCA sizes are constructed and several open questions are posed regarding the possible sizes of GCA quadruples.

However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. It was also shown that these UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. This proposed protocol has an entanglement cost of $4$, which is optimal since any entanglement-assisted protocol would require at least this much entanglement to distinguish the same UPB. Similarly, in $3 \otimes 4 \otimes 4$, an entanglement-assisted protocol with entanglement cost of $4$ was proposed to locally distinguish one such UPB, which is also the minimum entanglement required. It's also shown that any system with strong quantum nonlocality and a special property must have at least one base state in its corresponding UPB that is strongly nonlocal. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Ultimately, our method exhibits potential to maximize the speed of data collection for massive spectroscopic surveys. Although developed with SDSS-V in mind, the algorithm can be applied to any similar survey using astrobots. Additionally, future improvements may further enhance its performance. All code developed for this research is available on GitHub, along with instructions to apply the coordinate algorithm and target assignment scripts. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a result, the producer thread's performance, reliant on the consumer thread for data validation using the compiled code, is now driven by memory access speeds rather than execution time of the graph matching algorithm. This has a significant impact on the program's ability to process large inputs, enabling efficient detection of binary DAGs with 'nearly' linear time complexity. Additionally, this compilation technique proves valuable in optimizing the performance of other programs within the GP 2 ecosystem. Furthermore, as the GP 2 compiler is highly tunable, its potential to accelerate other graph-based programs is also explored, also highlighting prospects for application in program analysis outside the GP 2 ecosystem. This research is accompanied by a public demonstration of the GP 2 compiler in action, along with the source code for the compiler and the program it has optimized. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The proposed framework is also adaptable to a variety of contrastive learning techniques and loss functions, showcasing its versatility. Furthermore, we explored the framework's capability in dimensionality reduction, achieving results on par with traditional methods like PCA and MDS. The proposed framework is publicly available under the name ConTrA at https://github/RealTimeCode/ConTrA. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This category was previously mentioned as a potential source for quasiprimativity on one orbit within locally arc-transitive graphs. Our results specifically pinpoint the infinite number of bi-primative twisted wreath graphs that can be derived from locally arc-transitive twisted dihedra and orbit graphs of twisted wreath structures. Furthermore, we outline the automorphism group structure and the twisted dihedra family from which these graphs are derived. A concrete classification is given for all the twisted dihedra and their orbit graphs which can be derived from locally arc-transitive structures. This includes the description of twist values, quasiprimativity characteristics, and vertex stabilizers of the automorphism groups. Our theoretical framework allows us to classify a wide range of twisted dihedra and its orbit graphs as locally arc-transitive graphs with quasiprimitive automation groups. This classification includes twisted dihedra with twist values 4k, 4k+1, 4k+2, and 4k+3 and its orbit graphs that can be derived from locally arc-transitive structures. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. The study further highlights the importance of addressing optical camera characteristics, such as radial distortion, when handling high-resolution images, given that recent research has overstated the efficacy of methods based on synthetic data. The proposed framework, complete with simplified approaches and benchmark datasets, facilitates forward progress in the area of panoramic image stitching. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. As a testament to its flexibility, our model has already stimulated new hypotheses regarding the etiology of Parkinson's disease. As such, the code is openly available to encourage collaboration and feedback from the computational neuroscience community. It can be accessed via the GitHub repository https://github.com/kiyoharu/ParkinsonsModel. The associated data has been uploaded to the GitHub repository https://github.com/kiyoharu/ParkinsonsData. The research has been conducted in accordance with the 3R principles (replacement, reduction, refinement) established by William Russell and Colin Burt for the use of animals in scientific research. Moreover, the study has been approved by the Animal Use Committee and conducted under the guidance of experienced researchers. The research has been presented in the form of a lecture at the 2020 Australian and New Zealand Association for the Advancement of Science meeting. The code has since undergone substantial revisions, and the research is now submitted for peer review. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn appears to be directed towards the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy, a finding that has significant implications for the study of ultra/luminous infrared galaxies and the interaction of galaxies mergers. These results also provide a framework for predicting the output of new generation radio telescopes such as the Square Kilometre Array. This framework is based on predicting the output of low and medium band frequencies based on the output of active supermassive black holes. These predictions are particularly relevant for sources with low to medium redshifts. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our experiment employs a variety of evaluation metrics to compare the performance of multiple models, including an innovative comparison of diploid neural networks.
The outcome shows a surprising discovery where simpler models achieve comparable performance to complex diploid models, prompting further exploration into this phenomenon. 
The code and dataset are available for public access at https://github.com/ahmadsou/s1-zad1. 
In summary, our contribution to this research is twofold: first, we introduced an innovative method for weather detection using computer vision, second, we presented the RFS dataset that encompasses three categories of weather conditions. 
This study indicates that, despite the intricate nature of weather conditions, neural network-based models can achieve accurate classification using a single image, thereby potentially contributing to the development of safe automated transportation systems in diverse weather conditions.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code and model will be made available online.

Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our findings demonstrate the intricate relationships between different types of entanglement in Jaynes-Cummings systems. Our analysis yields a criterion for an unconnected system to become genuinely multipartite entangled, which is applicable to various Jaynes-Cummings setups. This research is compatible with current experimental capabilities, making it feasible to demonstrate multipartite entanglement using existing setups. Additionally, our study highlights the intricate relationships between distinct forms of entanglement within Jaynes-Cummings systems. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. This breakthrough marks a significant milestone in the development of the upgraded CMS pixel detector, set to play a crucial role in the LHC at a cumulative energy level of 13 TeV. The study highlights the detection's ability to handle typical multi-particle final states characteristic of quantum chromodynamics, in addition to detecting infrequent events involving isolated charged particles, absent or limited energy suppression, and anomalous track patterns. The findings provide evidence that the upgraded detector can accurately interpret data obtained on an industrial scale. In addition, researchers have validated the predicted performance of the upgraded detector equipped with improved readout software, namely the Data Drive Architecture. Specifically, it has been verified that this new architecture reduces data compression errors and associated secondary effects, resulting in a significant increase in acceptable luminosity levels, particularly for tackling complex physics scenarios. In conclusion, the results obtained from pilot module testing are consistent with predicted outcomes, thus providing a strong foundation for the upgraded forward pixel detector to deliver outstanding performance in future LHC research. In this study, the hit finding efficiency and track-residual patterns concluded that the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps can be applied to actual multi-particle events, yielding results that align with theoretical predictions. Consequently, this milestone is expected to pave the way for outstanding performance of the upgraded CMS pixel detector in future LHC experiments. A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density. Further research aims to enhance the method's precision and extend it to other observables. This approach may ultimately enable more comprehensive understanding of the glueball spectrum. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study demonstrates that the shadow radius can be an useful thermal entropy probe for understanding phase transition thermodynamics in black holes. Ultimately, we derive a formula for entropy based on shadow radius, which may be applicable across various non-linear YM gravity frameworks. This development paves the way for further investigation into the shadow radius-entropy relationship in both charged and neutral black holes within Einstein-power-Yang-Mills gravity. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for using shadow radii to examine phase transition behavior and entropy patterns in black holes. Additionally, this work offers a practical approach to estimating entropy from shadow radii, which can be validated through direct solution analysis. This new approach to understanding black hole thermodynamics may also be extended to other non-linear Yang-Mills gravity frameworks. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Additionally, we illustrate practical applications of this concept through examples involving multimode systems and suggesting that this approach can be extended to other continuous-variable systems. This research brings forward a new principle where specific properties of quantum states can be studied using the unique patterns of optical tomograms, ultimately simplifying the task of quantum state reconstruction.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and data generated by our approaches are made publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-dialogue-role-constraint. With this system, we envision a future where open-domain dialogue systems can effectively integrate diverse roles and maintain consistent conversation topics. Moreover, we hope to contribute to the development of more capable dialogue systems that can handle complex roles and tasks, thereby paving the way for them to be utilized in real-world applications. Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data. Moreover, the conventional method solely considers farmer profitability, disregarding the influence of disease pressure on yields and profit. To address these challenges, we developed a method using simulations to account for a limited number of observations and incorporated disease pressure's effect through a quantile regression model, applying this solution to strawberry disease management in Florida. The results showed that certain insect growth regulators can reduce the disease risk and increase yields and profit without significantly increasing production costs. Furthermore, the quantile regression model helped allocate variable costs according to disease pressure levels. This approach provides a statistical solution to the efficacy evaluation problem and raises the possibility of advancing this research to a mathematical programming model that can be solved with multiple data sets. In essence, we propose incorporating time as an explicit function in dynamic programming to address this challenge. The proposed approach has the potential to tackle more complex problems, such as modeling multiple decisions across different time periods and optimizing variables across various sensitivity analyses. The method we developed can likely be applied to a broader range of stochastic efficiency evaluations and may also be useful for addressing other decision-making challenges in agricultural research. The code for this study is available upon request. The new method was evaluated using eight different datasets and showed superior performance over the conventional method in terms of statistical significance in seven out of eight cases. The proposed approach provides a statistically meaningful way to estimate the efficacy of pesticide treatments despite a limited number of observations, and the results for strawberry disease management align with previous research finding the efficacy of certain insect growth regulators. The study's findings highlight the value of considering disease pressure's effect on yields and profit in efficiency evaluations and demonstrate the applicability of this method to a broad range of agricultural efficiency evaluations. The proposed approach has the potential to be a powerful tool for modeling complex decision-making problems in agricultural research, and the code for this study can serve as a starting point for developing more advanced solutions. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, an observation made from the model's analysis
indicates that navigation data from video subtitles can be useful for predicting
user views for a certain duration following the appearance of subtitles on the
screen. Based on these findings, a subtitle-driven dataset has been created and
made publicly available, followed by the introduction of a novel approach to
video subtitles, namely, the extraction of navigation keywords. With the aid of
these keywords, accurate prediction of user views is achieved, showcasing the
algorithm's effectiveness. The proposed approach's versatility is further
demonstrated through the incorporation of external navigation data, thereby
enabling increased precision in predicting user views. The entire process,
including the proposed model and keyword extraction, has been implemented
into a comprehensive dataset that is now made publicly available for the
benefit of the research community. The proposed approach's code and dataset
can be found at the following link: https://github.com/sonndinh-ait/360-Viewport- Prediction. The proposed approach has far-reaching potential for a range of applications
where video navigation data needs to be analyzed, such as video subtitles
analysis, healthcare, and automotive fields. The algorithm's code and the
subtitle-driven dataset are both available for the benefit of the technical
community at: https://github.com/sonndinh-ait/360-Viewport-P

This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. Along the way, we create a set of tools that can be used for surface-related problems, including the identification of global conclusions from local arguments and the demonstration of the existence of multiple solutions by constructing an infinite number of surfaces that satisfy particular conditions. We then illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a specific problem involving an infinite number of surfaces that satisfy specific criteria in relation to a given function. Our solution demonstrates the existence of at least two distinct surfaces, each with a unique property, that exist in a specific range but become non-existent outside of that range. We also establish a linear bounding surface to demonstrate the finite nature of a particular value as a result of our surface construction. Ultimately, we validate our approach by verifying the accuracy of our derived estimates through a process of review and modification. We believe that our work has the potential to contribute to a broader theory and encourage the development of additional strategies to expand our results to more comprehensive classes of surfaces. In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided. This involves the discovery that certain potentials satisfy a modified anisotropic Poisson equation, which can be analyzed using anisotropic maximal operator properties. We also introduce an anisotropic version of the Poincare inequality for one-dimensional spaces, along with an anisotropic version of the Sobolev inequality, which can be established through Riemannian flat metric approximation. These results represent a key breakthrough in solving the anisotropic Minkowski problem, the anisotropic Chern-Weil formula, and the anisotropic codazzi equation. Additionally, we explore specific examples, including the anisotropic minimization of solid cone volumes in Euclidean space, and the anisotropic willmore inequality for minimal surfaces in the Euclidean space. Lastly, we discuss the codazzi equation for submanifolds with curved boundaries in the Euclidean space, resulting in new results for the anisotropic codazzi equation in the presence of constant coefficients. We also derive new results for submanifolds with curved boundaries in the Euclidean space, along with new results for the anisotropic codazzi equation in the presence of non-constant coefficients. We conclude by exploring potential applications of these results to the codazzi equation for submanifolds with curved boundaries in the Euclidean space. We hope this research will lead to a better understanding of the codazzi equation and its connections to the anisotropic willmore inequality and the minkowski inequality. We also hope this research will also contribute to a better understanding of the anisotropic codazzi equation and its connections to the codazzi equation for submanifolds with curved boundaries in the Euclidean space. We believe this research is an important step towards a more comprehensive study of the codazzi equation and its connections to the anisotropic willmore inequality, the minkowski inequality, and the anisotropic codazzi equation. We look forward to seeing the results of this research being built upon in future studies. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. Unfortunately, this approach still leaves significant portions of relevant data unusable. This issue highlights the importance of developing strategies to handle such events in future similar experiments. Despite this challenge, the currently usable data allows for a violation limit of $d2\rho/dt^2 < 3.4 \times 10^{-20} \, \mathrm{g}/\mathrm{cm}s^2$ at a $95\%$ confidence level. This limit is anticipated to become even more stringent with advanced strategies to handle glitches. Furthermore, this experiment has achieved a level of accuracy that demonstrates the potential for future experiments aimed at understanding the weak equivalence principle in a gravitational environment. Additionally, Microscope has contributed to the development of a new technique for detecting the weak equivalence principle, which involves using gravitational waves generated by the movement of heavy cosmic objects as a source. This technique has the potential to improve the detection capabilities for gravitational waves in the low-frequency range. While the current study has focused primarily on glitches, there is also evidence suggesting that there may be longer-duration acceleration fluctuations, known as secular variations, that could have an impact on the principle test. To differentiate these events from glitches, the time of variation would need to be further analyzed. Given the complexity of this problem, it is recommended that future experiments take steps to reduce the uncertainty associated with the time of variation, including implementing more sophisticated detection algorithms for glitches to prevent them from affecting the principle test. Ultimately, this experiment has highlighted the importance of accounting for the environment and the satellite itself when interpreting test mass acceleration data, which involves considering a range of factors that can influence the results. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. These results are particularly relevant to the behavior of cells during chemotherapy treatments.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete. Specifically, we prove a graph G has a 2-strong shortest path cover if and only if it is 2-link forest-free, and provide an NP-certification for this condition. Additionally, we provide a 2-hops cover time-complexity upper bound of O(n^3), although the general k-hops cover problem appears NP-hard. Finally, we compare our results to existing strong shortest path cover research.
