Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of using a non-invasive BCI approach with high resolution recordings to control the most complex aspect of lower limb function – walking – and suggests that this system has the potential for safe integration with current prosthetic technologies. Nonetheless, numerous challenges must be overcome, including the need for recordings to be as accurate when taken from different BCI sessions (known as generalizability). In addition, the system would require real-time performance in a more dynamic walking state and have scalability issues when moved from a laboratory to a broader walking environment. Despite these obstacles, this study represents a significant step towards the development of a BCI-powered walking prosthetic device. It paves the way for further research aimed at addressing the identified limitations and showcases the potential for a game-changing technology that can safely and accurately be used for the complex control of lower limb function in humans. It also highlights the potential for this technology to be adapted for other costly and safe-to-operate systems that rely on significant user involvement, such as artificial arms and rehabilitation robots. It is essential that future studies address the issue of generalizability by conducting recordings over an extended period (>16 minutes) in a more dynamic environment and involving multiple participants. It is equally crucial that future research is focused on developing algorithms capable of providing safe and accurate level 2 control of walking, where the system can adapt to changes in real-time and is available for public scrutiny, to ensure that the technology is safe for public use and can be scaled up for an broader walking settings

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Consequently, we demonstrate that the Schreier graph corresponding to this component has a high chromatic number. Additionally, we find that if the group has a non-trivial, faithful action on a tree that is not a line, then there exists an arc in the graph $\Gamma$ whose corresponding Schreier graph has a high chromatic number. This result builds upon the work of Bestvester and Feinberg, and provides a negative answer to a question proposed by that pair. Our methods also contribute a new approach to analyzing the behavior of right-angled Artin groups within trees. This research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Alongside outstanding performance, DECENNT-generated graphs provide actionable insights for researchers and experts in various domains. Furthermore, DECENNT's code and datasets used are available for public access. In conclusion, DECENNT is an innovative model that leverages directed and dynamic graph representations to enhance performance in classification and prediction tasks. Additionally, DECENNT's grids are highly consistent with existing research findings and offer additional expert knowledge. Moreover, DECENNT is distinguishable due to its temporal attention mechanism that identifies crucial time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. DECENNT's code and datasets used are available for public access at https://github.com/ghulam-eiman/DECENNT. Our findings were achieved by training the model on a NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU. Any further inquiries can be directed to the author's email at [eiman@cs.umn.edu].

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The evaluation is conducted across a range of tree and network topologies, alongside assessments of retention rates for specific network features. A supplementary tool is also made available for readers to reproduce and extend the comparisons made in this study. Overall, our research offers a comprehensive overview and assessment of the capabilities of phylogenetic network generators, which is essential for informed choice and the guidance of future network generator development. The study is underpinned by an open-source platform that is comprised of the Python tools we employed in our analysis, along with a suite of interactive visualizations to aid in the comparison and contrast of different network generator outcomes. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed approach and associated dataset have the potential to contribute to various applications such as animal monitoring, sporting event analysis, and medical diagnosis using video data. The code and dataset are available for use at https://github.com/aishell1/biolocomotion_detection. The proposed method's ability to analyze the movement of individual parts of an object proves useful in biolocomotion detection, ensuring that the detected motion is consistent across different scales. By recognizing the unique combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion in biolocomotion, the developed approach outperforms alternative methods and provides accurate results on the created dataset. The acknowledged differences between the movement of biological and non-biological objects, coupled with the proposed method's accessibility and modifiable code, make it an suitable biolocomotion detection system. The recognition of the distinctive movement patterns of biolocomotion, along with the developed approach and associated dataset, facilitate further research into the detection of biolocomotion from video data. The proposed method's code and associated dataset can contribute to various applications such as animal monitoring, sporting event analysis, and medical diagnosis using video data. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. In our experiments, NN consistently outperformed other fast iterative methods in terms of accuracy and speed on both synthetic and real-world datasets. In particular, NN achieved a notable improvement in sparse systems and large non-sparse systems. In conclusion, the Nested Neumann method represents a premier solution for approximate matrix inversion, capable of efficiently processing large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion applications with minimal additional RAM. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our predictions can be validated using atomic or photonic lattice setups that incorporate binary disorders. These findings provide an expansion of the known properties of topological Anderson phases to include correlated disorders.

The proposed efficient algorithms for robust vector pooling and optimal transport could also find utility in other domains, such as computer vision and data analytics. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed approach incorporates molecular force generation and network reorganization through the use of thermodynamic limits of rate-based models and membrane protein dynamics informed by recent research. By integrating these elements, our model highlights the importance of their combined action in governing cellular spreading and reorientation over single fiber behavior. This suggests that higher-level network contractility, although essential, is not sufficient to explain cellular reorientation in response to sharp corners. Instead, this behavior relies on the accumulation of proteins during approach and subsequent network reorganization to facilitate reorientation. This phenomenon is illustrated through both numerical solution and biphasic experiment of fibroblast cell spreading in isolation, showcasing how cells efficiently navigate around obstacles due to their ability to adapt their membrane protein inventory. This leads to a unique cellular response to external stimuli known as path memory, where cells tend to follow a similar path in repeated passages, attributed to the persistent accumulation of membrane proteins in response to local gradient generation during initial approach. This further highlights the vast implications this underlying mechanism has for higher-level cellular behavior in more intricate environments. This report on our multi-faceted framework for the cellular spreading and reorientation builds upon our initial research, providing a comprehensive overview that includes a detailed description of the underlying principles, model developments, and results for both single-layer actin networks and membrane protein dynamics. This discourse also involves a discussion on the identified key factors influencing cellular reorientation and the intricate interplay they have with external stimuli. Consequently, this multi-facetal approach for cellular spreading and reorientation offers a promising framework for further investigation into the intricate relationships between cells, tissues, and their surrounding microenvironments. This approach has the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of complex cellular responses to external cues in multiscalar systems consisting of single fiber contractility, actin networks, membrane protein dynamics, and lipid membranes. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By unveiling the underlying mechanisms of money trail circulation, our research provides valuable insights into the temporal cyclic transfers within cryptocurrency blockchains, offering a potential tool for developers to enhance payment security and prevent malicious activities. Furthermore, our approach to analyzing temporal graphic structures can serve as a foundation for investigating other complex temporal systems. Additionally, we introduce a new concept called the Earth Mover's Distance with Multiple Sources for comparing the cyclic transfer patterns across different blockchain datasets. In conclusion, our groundbreaking analysis of money trails within cryptocurrency blockchains reveals significant value in shaping the future of secure payment systems and informing research on cyclic transfer patterns in complex temporal graphs. In our investigation, we centered on Ethereum but our approach is applicable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we demonstrated that using a decoder trained on a virtual environment can be highly beneficial when incorporated into a larger learning system interacting with the code environment. Additionally, we developed a decoder that can be trained to minimize two types of errors: measurement errors and logical error, and we found that doing so may actually decrease the measurement error threshold of quantum computation. However, increasing the number of decoders interacting with the code environment does not seem to follow the curse of dimensionality, and we suggest that this phenomenon has implications for the scalability of quantum computation. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. However, the analysis of interaction effects reveals that the Scrum method can mitigate the negative impact of remote working on project success. Therefore, we propose that using Scrum from home increases project success by increasing competence and facilitating the fulfillment of the relatedness need. Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Conversely, antiparticle distributions show minimal dependence on event-shape engineering.  Furthermore, antiparticle contributions to the elliptic flow coefficient are found to differ negatively from charged hadrons, a result consistent with findings at lower energies.  Additionally, study of the vector flow pattern, facilitated by the integration of the Charge Independent Condition into the hydrodynamic analysis, reveals that the event-shape selection's impact on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also determined is that the ratio of radial and elliptic flow patterns depends on the transverse grade of particles, with higher transverse transverse flows observed in events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow.  Finally, study of charged hadron distributions in events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, compared to average elliptic flow events, indicates that events exhibiting higher elliptic flow are characterized by higher average temperatures and density at the moment of thermalization.  These results provide insight into the interrelations between radial and elliptic flow, as well as the properties of the initial state condition that influence elliptic flow in nuclear collisions.  Also, study of the same phenomena at higher energy, specifically at a 2.76 TeV collision energy, is anticipated.  Finally, study of event-shape engineering in lead-lead collisions, specifically at a 2.76 TeV collision energy, is anticipated to be beneficial in furthering our understanding of the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient in nuclear collisions. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. As such, this study does not provide practical power control advice, rather it offers an exploration of extremal gain characterizations through highly abstract analyses. As an interesting side note, this study found that extremal gain characterizations hold similar values when considering other methods of network organization, such as hierarchical structures. As such, it is suggested that further research into networks characterized by extreme gain values could lead to further theoretical insights. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, our multiple-time-step algorithm provides a significant improvement for accurate simulations of complex sediment transport by incorporating particle collisions. This algorithm can be applied to various particle collision models and will play a crucial role in efficiently simulating complex sediment transport simulations. Furthermore, this research reveals the implications of collision time steps on sediment entrainment and turbulence. In addition, our algorithm has been published as an open-source code on GitHub for the community to use. In the future, we plan to continue developing this algorithm and applying it to simulate other phenomena involving particle collisions. Lastly, we look forward to receiving feedback and new collision models that can be integrated into our algorithm. Our algorithm has been successfully tested using the PHI-based Fronthub system at the University of Texas at Austin. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. Additionally, we derive the highest power of $2$ that can be achieved under this criterion and determine specific examples corresponding to powers of $2$ of $3$ and $4$. Furthermore, we explore the potential for similar theories to apply to other types of numbers, such as quadratic fields and cyclotomic fields. Lastly, we propose two open questions in this realm.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. To validate the simulation-based findings, a physical one-legged hopping robot was built and tested. While the physical robot exhibited similar performance in tandem with the simulation, it suffered from significant tracking errors and could not repeat the level of precision achieved in the simulated environment. Nonetheless, the feedback controller on the physical robot reduced errors compared to the feedforward control system, albeit to a lesser extent. The discrepancies between the simulated and actual performances can be attributed to various factors, including but not limited to, the limitations of the RFT model's applicability to real-world scenarios. In conclusion, this project successfully designed, implemented, and tested a force control system on a one-legged hopping robot in a simulated soft ground environment, and subsequently, the controller was applied to the physical robot despite its limitations. The feedback controller, especially when employed with a larger foot size, exhibited its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces. The approach presented herein provides a potential framework for addressing the challenges associated with legged locomotion on deformable terrain. The source code associated with this project is available online at https://github.com/AmirHoseinKhoei/One-Legged-Hopping-Robot. The research reported in this paper has been financially supported by the Canadian Institute for Advanced Study, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the Iran National Science Foundation

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. These results are presented in a table for several mesons. Additionally, the model is extended to account for mesons containing quark-anti-quark pairs of the same flavor, enabling the calculation of strange meson form factors. Calculated values for the scalar $f_0$, pseudoscalar $\eta'$, and vector $\rho$ mesons are detailed. These results demonstrate how the model predicts the magnitude of form factor values, which become larger for mesons with higher mass. This development pattern is attributed to the increasing mass of meson components with spin $1/2$. The model also facilitates investigation of the flavor symmetry by comparing form factor values of distinct flavor mesons. It is found that the difference in form factor values for quark masses of the order of the actual mass of the up and strange quarks is approximately 0.1 GeV. This finding demonstrates the model's capability to evaluate the flavor symmetry effect on the form factor through the variation of quark mass within the solvable mass range. As an alternative method, the contact interaction model also allows the derivation of form factors from the Bethe-Salpeter equation in a semi-analytical manner. It is possible to obtain dressed inter-quark interactions without resolving the BSE. By minimizing the eigenvalue of the one-body operator in the BSE, the form factor can be determined without full solution of the BSE. This approach is demonstrated by calculating the form factor of the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons. The minimum eigenvalue values of the one-body operator for these two mesons differ by approximately 0.3 GeV, indicating a tendency of the mass of the $\omega$ meson being greater than the $\rho$ meson. However, it is also pointed out that this approach has the limitation of being unable to distinguish between the mass of the $\omega$ and $\rho$ mesons due to the failure to solve the mass difference between the two in the gap equation

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. Furthermore, the droplet's oscillatory behavior could be tailored to modify the surrounding air's physical properties, thus potentially enriching the physics involved. The current study focuses on exploring the droplet's effects on the transportation of particulate matter in the airborne phase. A numerical model was utilized to analyze the droplet's interactions with the surrounding air, revealing how the oscillations alter the circulation patterns and affect the aerosol's distribution. The results show that the droplet's size, electric field strength, and frequency of oscillation significantly influence the aerosol's behavior, resulting in the formation of accumulation zones behind the droplet and the increased transport of particulate matter into the droplet's vicinity. The research offers insights into the droplet-airborne particle interactions and could have implications for understanding related phenomena, such as the transport of dust behind moving droplets in certain celestial events. The study's findings are also relevant to situations involving the interaction of droplets with aerosol clouds in natural processes, such as rainfall, as well as in engineering applications, such as coal power plant flue gas washing. The research is further expanded to explore the interaction of the droplet with flowing aerosol clouds, employing a numerical model that incorporates the effects of the droplet on the surrounding air while accounting for the droplet's oscillatory behavior. The study reveals how the droplet's size, electric field strength, and frequency of oscillation influence the aerosol's circulation patterns and result in the transportation of particulate matter into the droplet's accumulation zones behind the droplet. The research offers insights into the droplet-airborne particle interactions and could have implications for understanding related phenomena, such as the transport of dust behind moving droplets in certain celestial events. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. As NLP models continue to rise in prominence, it is imperative to address the negation challenge to ensure their effectiveness in real-world applications. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Additionally, we developed a visualization tool to present the inferred themes and hierarchies in a clear and explorable manner, making it easier to navigate and mine insights from large information networks. This approach and accompanying tool are available as an open source system under the Apache License, Version 2.0, and can be found at http://sourceforge.net/projects/hdtm/. Furthermore, we include three preprocessed Wikipedia datasets to facilitate further research in this domain. By leveraging the distributed processing capabilities of HDTM, we extracted 502 topics from the Wikipedia dataset, and the corresponding hierarchy can be viewed at http://www.7ism.com/hdwm/. Furthermore, we applied this approach to analyze the CNN News network, employing a mixed strategy to combine topic models and establish a hierarchy, and the resulting hierarchy can be seen at http://www.7ism.com/hdzn/. Lastly, we explore the practical implications of this approach in the context of two real-world applications. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The associated quantum quench dynamics span multiple degrees of freedom and develop intricate patterns of correlation over time. The neural network's ability to analyze and replicate the annealing gap's behavior from quench data is demonstrated across distinct Hamiltonian parameters and scenario variations, including situations where the quench yields equilibrium phases that differ from those reached through quantum annealing. The latter case represents the most challenging scenario for the algorithm. The proposed approach opens up possibilities for improving quantum annealing by exploiting the quench state's dynamic properties or investigating other quench protocols that could lead to a deeper understanding of quantum annealing dynamics in complex systems. The statistical tools employed in this study also provide a valuable resource for analyzing the annealing gap's behavior from a quantum state perspective. The quantum quench state can be used as a starting point to investigate how equilibrium phases are reached in quantum systems, while the associated correlation structures can offer insights into the systems' underlying properties and interactions. The approach discussed in the study applies to continuous-time quantum annealing and quench protocols, and the associated Hamiltonians can incorporate time-dependent spin interactions or Boolean classical covering problems. The realistic simulation scenarios involve finite annealing periods, spin decay, and spin-spin interaction loss, and the quantum quench state's duration is set to the system's relaxation time. The statistical analysis employs trained neural networks with input quench data to replicate the annealing gap's behavior across various Hamiltonian parameters

A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. It also highlights challenges associated with assessing partial process runs and discusses potential applications of these methods across various disciplines. Additionally, it offers novel insights into conducting conformance checks with partial process data and presents practical solutions using publicly available software. Lastly, it paves the way for future research topics related to conformance checking. This research was conducted with professionals in the field of business process management and utilized real-world event data to test its methods. It offers techniques that can be employed to detect deviations in process runs and assess the quality of these processes. It also offers potential solutions to challenges associated with assessing partial process runs and conducting conformance checks with initial segments of process runs. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Includes discussions on both the limitations of such one-band approximations and
possible experimental avenues for validation. 
Additionally, a brief exploration into possible phase diagrams with additional
bands is also presented. 
A general discussion on the general lack of understanding of the true multi-band
nature of the Hamiltonian through experimental means is included.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Lastly, the results are validated through direct numerical simulations.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling the derivation of wind-speed dependent wave-slope probabilities up to 15 m/s. Our method reevaluates Cox and Munk's methodology for determining wave-slope probability distribution from photographs of sun glints, offering an alternative, more robust approach for retrieving parameters of a probability distribution function. Our results for wave slope statistics are comparable to previous findings, yet our data exhibits reduced uncertainties that pinpoint potential discrepancies between observed wave behaviors and previous models at moderate wind speeds. Our study also highlights how wave slope statistics change as wind speed increases, specifically noting the impact on skewness, kurtosis coefficients, and the behavior of updown wind asymmetry. Notably, our results indicate that waves become more peaked and positively sloped with increasing wind speed. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that wind speed can significantly affect the orientation of waves, with shifts occurring in moments of the probability distribution that describe how waves orient themselves in relation to the wind. Our study also explores relationships between wave slopes and wind speed, specifically noting how these relationships evolve with different wind speeds, as characterized by the behavior of intersections between curves representing different stages of wave development. Our research identifies distinct thresholds at wind speeds of approximately 7 and 13 m/s, with changes occurring across these milestones. We propose that these thresholds might reflect changes in the breakdown of waves into different components, such as wind-induced capillary, wind-driven wave, and wave waves, with potential implications for our understanding of turbulence in this context. Our study provides a theoretical basis for modeling the effects of wind-driven waves and suggests potential applications to inform numerical models used to study the interactions between oceans and atmospheres. Finally, our approach can also contribute to improving the interpretation of radiance data, specifically utilizing the diversity of available spectral channels to study physical phenomena that influence the appearance of oceans from space. Our approach can likely be adapted for studying other fluids, such as rivers and oceans during nighttime, when other factors come into play. Our study sets the stage for a series of subsequent studies that can further explore the characteristics of wave slopes, as well as other fluid dynamics, by combining multi-band photometric data with numerical models. When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Concurrent testing
also enables continuous integration and continuous deployment methods. Experimental
results using an open source database demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. We also explore possible applications to other software systems. The implementation is available online. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We demonstrate the applicability of our research by utilizing the anti Tai mapping lower bound as a cut in the integer program designed to solve the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem. We present empirical results obtained by applying our algorithm to popular benchmark datasets. We also investigate the average-case complexity of the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem by conducting statistical analysis of randomly generated datasets. We demonstrate that even in cases where one tree is significantly larger than the other, the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping can be computationally demanding despite the large size difference. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. What is remarkable about this discovery, is that hidden functionalities could not only be activated by the presence of specific input features, but also arose during the normal training process without the need for maliciously modified training data, thus highlighting the necessity to reevaluate the reliability of neural networks in various machine learning applications. Through experimental research, concrete evidence has been found that the presence of this backdoor functionality is unaffected by various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification, thus highlighting its widespread applicability. In addition, three distinct machine learning tasks have been found to exhibit this backdoor functionality, thus indicating it is a widespread phenomenon. In response to these discoveries, several security measures have been implemented to prevent the emergence of this backdoor functionality in neural networks, thus providing a basis for further exploration into this topic. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This research has implications for future missions, such as the PLATO satellite, where a similar variation in angular diameter may influence cone corrections. In this case, the effect on the zero point is likely significantly greater, possibly in the tenths of a microarcsecond, although this depends heavily on specific mission configurations and aspects of its data processing. In both scenarios, this study highlights the importance of integrating general relativity's effects into mission simulations and data analysis to ensure the highest possible accuracy. Finally, we propose that, regardless of the outcome of this research, future missions should prioritize investigating the impact of PPN parameters on astronomical measurements. This could be achieved by conducting in-flight validations against the predicted effects of gravitational phenomena, such as particular high-accuracy tests of general relativity's influences on light deflection, influenced significantly by the position of the observer, the observer's velocity, and the structure of the gravitational source, among other factors. This represents an exceptional opportunity to contribute to our understanding of general relativity's implications for gravitational physics. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Moreover, we show that these methods can generate robust models that accurately predict long-term behavior and shift towards the systems' stable states following temporary deviations. Notably, the models we create are inherently multi-scale and consistent with the systems' gradual evolution towards their underlying structure. Additionally, we introduce a new metric that quantifies the systems' gradient complexity and demonstrates its applicability through numerical systems and a real-world application involving financial systems. Furthermore, we explore the systems' conditional stability by analyzing the impact of sudden changes on their behavior and provide a theoretical formulation for their stability based on the systems' underlying structure. Through these methods and the proposed metric, we aim to provide a framework that facilitates the development of concise and coherent theories for complex systems. Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. A potential experimental implementation of these models is also discussed, including the possibility of organizing the interacting solitons into an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. This could be achieved by manipulating the optical-lattice potential to model a harmonic oscillator with two eigenstates, thereby enabling the reliable production of self-accelerating solitons. Additionally, this work offers a theoretical framework that can be applied to other systems with similar properties. This includes the possibility of accurately modeling the interaction between two-dimensional solitons and the formation of stable, self-accelerating structures in harmonic lattices. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. SIMC 2.0's enhanced design provides enhanced privacy and performance for various ML models, including support for 136 voters in binary logistic regression and 13 voters in multiclass logistic regression. The optimized protocol also enables secure inference for critical applications, such as image classification, with runtime comparable to existing solutions. The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This technique does not rely on the structure of domain elements and can be closely linked to a method proposed by Hensel and Newman. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Additionally, it has the potential to make spectroscopy more accessible, enabling a wider range of researchers to conduct advanced spectroscopy while reducing the overall setup cost. 

As part of the Galactic Exoplanet Survey, the Silicon Cross-Correlation Spectrograph is an innovative instrument that utilizes a high-resolution spectrograph and a pair of flat field detectors to conduct narrowband optical spectroscopy. This instrument was designed to detect exoplanets by detecting atomic hydrogen in the interstellar medium and detecting molecular gas in the host star's atmosphere. 

The instrument consists of three key components: a photonic device, a cross-correlation software, and a data analysis tool. The photonic device is responsible for splitting the light into multiple spectral components, and the software performs cross-correlation using a template spectrum, and the data analysis tool determines the detection criteria based on the instrument's performance. 

The instrument was tested under various conditions and detected molecular gas in 79.2% of low-metallicity star candidates and 27.3% of SMC dwarf spheroidal galaxy members, demonstrating its effectiveness. The instrument is currently undergoing further testing and optimization to increase its sensitivity.

A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Moreover, the study showed that the rotation rate's highest possible value, above which turbulent flows become strongly non-Newtonian, lies significantly below the threshold for bi-stability. This finding is particularly notable as it identifies a distinct "middle ground" of inertial wave turbulence between the strongly non-rotating regime of two-dimensional turbulence and the bi-stable geostrophic vortices in the strongly rotating regime. Additionally, the research provided the frequency spectrum and energy spectra for both the cascading wave modes and the largest scales of motion, which play a crucial role in determining the turbulent flows' spatial intensity. Furthermore, it was discovered that the wave turbulence exhibits a characteristic of "multi-pulse" structure, which is a result of the interplay between the spreading waves and the rotating shear flow. This multi-pulse structure is displayed through diagrams that illustrate how the amplitude of the waves varies in relation to their frequency, showing distinct peaks corresponding to different "pulses". Lastly, it was found that the wave turbulence's own downscale cascade contributes significantly to its own generation, thus providing a major underlying mechanism for its existence. However, it was also found that the time of the largest scales of motion is twice as long as the time of the waves, which leads to a significant impact on the turbulent flows' spatial intensity. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of inertial wave turbulence and its bi-stable counterpart, geostrophic vortices, for the first time. It offers a perspective that views the two regimes as two branches of a single concept, the concept of bi-stability, which is separated by a critical rotation rate. It also highlights the role of the two regimes in the life cycle of turbulent flows, which starts with the destruction of geostrophic vortices and continues until the formation of new geostrophic vortices.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Furthermore, as a secondary benefit, mental health treatment appears to lower the odds of an offender being arrested again within a three-year frame by 24 percent or almost 8 points.  In addition, it seems that mental health treatment reduces the odds of an offender being convicted of another crime or sentenced to a more severe penalty even if it is not immediately apparent.  Therefore, connecting offenders with necessary mental health services as part of their rehabilitation is crucial for reducing their likelihood of returning to the justice system.  Therefore, ensuring access to these services is essential for reducing future crime rates and overcoming healthcare disparities within the criminal justice system. To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This will mark the largest and most complex FPGA design installed at the CERN site. This paper provides an in-depth look at the design, performance, and production aspects of this cutting-edge project. It offers a unique behind-the-scenes glimpse at the challenges faced and the innovative solutions implemented by the team, as well as the outstanding results achieved with a level of precision and reliability demanded by the ATLAS experiment's stringent standards. This development represents a major milestone in the history of high-energy physics' most complex detector systems, as it pushes the envelope of what is possible with custom digital design. This breakthrough is set to have a significant impact on future detector upgrades and research projects in this field. This project has also paved the way for other ATLAS L1 trigger upgrade projects, such as the global trigger and the upgrade of the muon trigger, which are currently in the design phase. This development's influence extends beyond ATLAS as well, as it has inspired other CERN research projects such as the LHCb's hadron level trigger upgrade and the future CMS Level 1 trigger upgrade projects, with several other particle accelerator projects in the United States and Europe also showing interest in its design and performance. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method's efficiency is demonstrated by estimating $\eta_G$ compared to traditional methods such as kernel-based methods and neural network-based methods in terms of mean squared error. The proposed method's performance on a genetic study dataset and an economic study dataset is also presented. The results show that GMLE can be an effective tool in practicing statistics for estimating population parameters when individual data is available along with corresponding sample data. The code for the methods discussed in this work is available online. The work also introduces a novel algorithm for computing the unique step function obtained from sorting the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$, which is applicable beyond the mixing distribution context. The work concludes by discussing potential directions for future research, especially on the statistical inference side. The work is supported by NSF DMS 1513474 and also includes a discussion on the relationship between the mixing distribution and the density function $f(y|\theta)$. The work is relevant to various real-world applications and is accompanied by a novel algorithm for computing the unique step function obtained from sorting the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$. The work also provides an innovative approach to estimating $\eta_G$ and the results are demonstrated on multiple datasets. The method's efficiency is compared to other methods, including kernel-based methods and neural network-based methods, which shows the potential of GMLE to be an effective tool in practicing statistics. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms. The dataset is further enhanced by introducing a new evaluation metric called diversity score, which measures the degree of structure and proximity preservation in node embeddings. The diversity score is used to conduct a comparative study of six well-known node embedding techniques. The results show that the performance of these algorithms varies significantly with different attraction strategies and community detection methods, which can influence the diversity score. Consequently, when selecting node embedding algorithms for social networks, the choice should be based on the specific requirements of the application, considering factors like classification performance and modeling of graph structure and proximity.
