A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also helps us understand why cracking often occurs in a specific pattern - typically in segments - by looking at the distribution of cluster sizes. When we change the rate at which the particles reassemble, for example, by changing the viscosity of the fluid, we see a clear change in the size of cluster sizes, which is in line with our theoretical predictions. Our findings have broader implications, giving us insights into the breakdown of other types of floating materials that break down over long periods of time. Our research shows that both the breakdown of materials and the size of their components can be heavily influenced by the interplay of timescales that are fundamentally different from the time it takes for the material to break apart. This understanding can be applied to a wide range of situations, from the breakdown of comets to the formation of planets. Our research also highlights the importance of considering the interplay between timescales that are both very fast and very slow in our efforts to better understand these phenomena. Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%. Notably, our method successfully reduced the gap between grades, especially between Moderate and Severe, and also effectively handled imbalance and lesion presence. Overall, our innovative techniques such as Contrastive Learning, Mixup, and lesion-sensitive pre-training, enabled our model to excel in COVID-19 severity detection. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code and model weights are available online.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. Moreover, the predicted phase diagram highlights the presence of a 1/3-magnetization plateau, contributing to the unique properties of this honeycomb lattice system. The unique combination of weak anisotropy and high entropy of ground state makes GdInO3 an exciting candidate for quantum magnetism, while its positive specific heat and entropy further attest to its intrinsic magnetic frustration. This frustration, coupled with the absence of spin-dimer character, elevates GdInO3 to a premier example of a quasitwo-dimensional quantum magnetism. This study provides a comprehensive foundation for exploring the exotic phases of this material under applied pressure or light, leading to potential breakthroughs in our understanding of quasitwo-dimensional quantum magnetism. Ultimately, further research is required to fully unearth the intriguing characteristics of this fascinating honeycomb lattice system. This work is also relevant to the ongoing discussion on whether honeycomb lattice materials can exhibit true 1/3-magnetization plateau transitions, as observed in triangular-lattice systems. While the current phase diagram of GdInO3 does not offer a definitive answer, this question remains a motivating factor for the ongoing and planned experiments on this material. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, this EFX fairness condition holds in a weakened form, whereas we demonstrated an example of a mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations for any number of agents, where an allocation that is fair up to one good does not exist. Our investigation offers several generalizeable questions for further research. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV. Furthermore, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can reach complementarity with leading dark matter experiments, such as LUX, but with the added benefit of being able to detect dark matter at much lower masses. In addition, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can achieve the projected limits of next-generation experiments, such as GDS, even when concentrations of radioactive contaminants are high, specifically above the threshold where contemporary direct detection experiments face significant background challenges due to the presence of radioactive elements in the detectors, such as 232Th in silicon. The capabilities of paleo-detectors can further be enhanced by combining the results from multiple samples to achieve a greater understanding of the dark matter interactions at various scales, such as the density distribution and the momentum spectrum. The capabilities of paleo-detectors can potentially lead to a deeper comprehension of dark matter and its interactions with ordinary matter, especially in the direct detection arena, by offering a unique perspective that complements the findings of other experiments. The potential of paleo-detectors to make significant contributions to the field of direct dark matter detection encourages further research into this experimental technique. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model available on open source platforms, we hope to stimulate the development of more effective unsupervised re-identification methods that can utilize large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video. At the very least, the dataset that we created consists of 30,000 distinct images spanning 1,436 unique identities, thereby representing a significant expansion of currently available re-identification datasets. Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses. Nonetheless, our most accurate parameter set originates from the traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo method, specifically the "bridged" version that harmonizes data and model differences. As a significant improvement, we found the implementation of two robust sampling methods for marginal likelihood estimation in the context of pulsar timing array data. Notably, we discovered the influence of sampling methods on the logarithmic marginal likelihood, a key indicator of model fit, and advise researchers to integrate results from multiple samplers for cross-validation in complex data sets. Ultimately, we expect ongoing searches to yield significant signals in pulsar timing array data in the future. Until then, it is crucial to continually evaluate and refine analysis tools to ensure the most accurate interpretations of data. As a step in this direction, we made our analysis code publicly available for replication and future research applications. Additionally, we invite the scientific community to benefit from using our publicly accessible analysis toolkits for cross-validation and other purposes. Furthermore, we plan to monitor and refine our findings through regular updates in response to new data releases. As such, we encourage open communication and feedback from researchers and data analysts in this field. Our publicly accessible code can be found at https://github.com/PMF2018/PTA_analysis_code.git. We look forward to contributing to the advancement of pulsar timing array data analysis through collaboration with researchers and the broader scientific community. Heard for our evaluation of sampling methods, as well as the open-data policy adopted by the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, the Arecibo Pulsar Timing Array, the NANOGrav Physical Model, and the EPTA Tables, and are supportive of ongoing efforts to make more pulsar timing array data publicly available. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. The implications of our study for the development of linear combinations of two quark currents that effectively target the pion are also considered. Given that the quark current combinations in question share similarities with those employed in recent studies of lattice QCD, our findings are likely to be of interest to those investigating the physics of the meson delta-meson system.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. A supplementary model that incorporates a simple mechanism for how people form opinions based on luck in job success is also presented. This model fits the data closely and provides a possible framework for future research. Unlike existing models of opinions on inequality, this model reacts differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income, is consistent with the established literature on the effect of luck on income, and accurately fits the data collected. The model is then used to examine the impact of inequality and the probability of luck influencing worker outcomes on redistribution policies in a hypothetical society. The results show that participants want to reduce the gap in earnings, specifically the effect of luck, particularly when it comes to job success, which they distinguish from overall income. The model predicts that participants would redistribute a larger percentage of the difference between luck-free high-earnings incomes into the lower earnings group. The model also predicts that increasing the probability of luck influencing worker outcomes reduces the desire for redistribution, as does the level of overall inequality. The model can be extended to consider multiple sources of luck with different probabilities and degrees of distinction between various outcomes. The study's findings provide a starting point for the discussion of a broader research agenda that aims to model opinions on inequality in the US. The agenda is set against the backdrop of the apparent disconnect between laboratory research conducted in the US and real-world inequality trends in the US. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The comprehensive studies of our approach on the 3D MultiAgentHero Dataset reveal that our method not only outperforms current benchmarks but also showcases robust performance in scenarios with substantial differences in player performance. Additionally, our approach successfully mitigates the negative impact of ineffective agents on the team by prioritizing high-quality experiences. The successful extraction of high-quality trajectories from offline datasets also enables our approach to achieve notable improvements when applied to new task settings, demonstrating the framework's potential for true offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our framework further enables the prediction of nuclear star clusters' mass-distribution and their potential merger partners, also accounting for the effect of pair-instability supernovae. This prediction shows a significant overlap with the characteristics of GW190521. Our study provides a foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of Population III binary remnants' development into nuclear star clusters, shedding light on the origins of heavy elements within these clusters, as well as the cosmic distribution of Population III binary remnants themselves. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Consequently, the structure of new knowledge relies heavily on existing knowledge. Furthermore, researchers observed that disciplines with a higher knowledge amount (e.g. physics, biology, chemistry) demonstrate a notable slowdown before this threshold, in contrast to disciplines like engineering, earth sciences, and medical sciences with lower knowledge amounts, which do not exhibit this slowdown. The findings suggest that the value of new knowledge is not equally distributed and is influenced by structural barriers, where disciplines with greater knowledge amounts experience a greater increase in new knowledge but only once the literature plateau is surpassed. Additionally, the data indicate that the speed of knowledge production accelerates in direct proportion to the existing knowledge amount, indicating that productivity itself is a key driver of productivity. Ultimately, the study provides a definitive answer to the question of how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement and highlights the underlying structural barriers that govern the evolution of scientific knowledge. The index of knowledge amount also offers a new framework for analyzing the development of scientific disciplines and is applicable to any area of research and citation networks. The introduction of the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI) also enables a more precise measurement of the return on investment for research projects and can serve as a key performance indicator (KPI) in evaluating the effectiveness of research initiatives. The study's methods and findings may prove useful in informing strategies to accelerate scientific knowledge production and ultimately advance the development of scientific disciplines as a whole. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical basis for developing secure, dual hop OFDM communication systems that can adapt to changing connectivity scenarios. Simulation results are promising and indicate that our proposed methods can deliver substantial security gains without incurring significant performance degradation. Additionally, our research highlights the potential for further improving performance by incorporating time domain processing techniques. As such, this investigation paves the way for future studies on optimization of communication protocols under connectivity constraints. Meanwhile, our results remain applicable across various multiuser scenarios, including those involving orthogonal space division multiple access and frequency division multiple access architectures. Lastly, our methodological approach is equally relevant to other nonconvex optimization problems in the field of communications and networking.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin entangled states upon applying a single control pulse. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of emitters selectively interacting with distinct channels via light-matter coupling. These capabilities provide the foundation for implementing quantum operations among protected photons and generating complex, entangled states of light within these topological channels. Ultimately, this paves the way for realizing robust quantum computations and communication protocols. Additionally, we identify potential applications for this system, including the creation of self-localized quantum emitters capable of separating into distinct, entangled states upon application of a pulse. This scenario presents a groundbreaking example of a robust, self-localizing phenomenon driven by spontaneous emission. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
As a result, researchers and developers can conduct in-depth experiments with ease, making it possible to thoroughly evaluate the performance of virtual agents even when they perform subpar. 
We created TextWorldExpress by applying various techniques of acceleration, including motion planning, graph optimization, and translation to more efficient simulation engines. 
Alongside the text games themselves, we also developed a suite of tools to help agents learn faster and adapt better to new challenges. 
Ultimately, this research takes a significant step towards creating a more efficient and effective method of evaluating virtual agents by assessing them in realistic, prolonged scenarios. 
We publicly release both TextWorldExpress and its accompanying tools to facilitate further development and testing of virtual agents. 
The accelerated versions of the games are currently available on nevermind.ai, and the full text-based challenges can be found on GitHub under the textworldexpress label. 
We would like to thank all the researchers whose challenges and agents have enabled this research, and we hope TextWorldExpress proves useful in taking virtual agents to the next level. 
We have already achieved promising results using our accelerated versions, and we look forward to seeing how other researchers can utilize and build upon this research. 
In particular, we have utilized reinforcement learning to demonstrate substantial improvements in agent performance, and we believe this is merely the beginning of a new era in text-based games.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. As a consequence, this research leads to a major breakthrough in the development of hardware accelerators for LSTM-based video recognition models, making it possible to apply this technology in actual applications. Lastly, the designed hardware and algorithms have been implemented on an FPGA platform and the detailed design can be found on an FPGA board that is accessible via a public repository. In summary, this research involves a comprehensive exploration of LSTM algorithms and hardware architectures in conjunction with a novel integrated design that targets high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks for video recognition. As a result, this work achieves a significant advancement in the area and paves the way for further innovations in deep learning algorithms and hardware collaborations. In addition, the customized FDHT-LSTM architecture and hardware accelerator have been made openly accessible via a public repository along with the source code for the algorithm and hardware, which can be found under the directory 'FDHT-LSTM'. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. On the other hand, in theories with a smooth spectrum, we propose that the symmetry should be extended to a higher group, such as SO(N+1), where the dimension of the operator exhibits a linear relationship with the charge under this symmetry, without any further specification. The proposed conjecture provides the framework for formulating the Weak Gravity Conjecture within the context of conformal field theory and also offers the opportunity to formulate additional hypotheses concerning the gravitational sector. To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. We find that compared to full unitary evolution, using an approximate unitary propagator has a negligible impact on MSQITE's performance, except when the unitary propagator is extremely small. We also establish that folding the spectrum does not benefit the model-space QITE and propose quantum-time-evolution-based alternatives to fold-spectrum QITE. Finally, we discuss potential applications of MSQITE to folded-spectrum QITE and discuss its potential advantages for simulating systems with multiple charge states or intermingled energy spectra. We demonstrate the feasibility of MSQITE on a superconducting quantum processor, achieving an excited state accuracy of 0.17 within 0.01 units of the energy threshold on a single qubit. We anticipate that this model-space QITE approach will become a powerful standard for quantum state simulations on near-term quantum devices.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. A critical component of our analysis involves the use of a random polynomial model, drawing inspiration from the work of Diaconis and Shashoua. By examining the properties of this model, we are able to derive insights into the Galois groups of various polynomials and systems of polynomials. Specifically, when considering the composition of two irreducible polynomials with distinct coefficients, the resulting Galois group exhibits a complex structure, mirroring the structure of the free product of two finite groups in the context of permutation groups. As a result, we are able to derive bounds on the absolute Galois group of the field obtained by composing two finite fields, using a system of polynomials, and evaluating the connected component of the identity in the Galois group of a composite field. Additionally, we explore connections between the Galois groups of the positive characteristic version and its zero-characteristic counterpart. The analysis of the structure of the Galois group of the composite polynomial enables us to formulate conjectures in relation to the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the autocorrelation of polynomials, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. The study of the Galois groups of the positive characteristic version may also lead to a deeper understanding of the absolute Galois group of the polynomial ring k(t)[x] over the integers, the rational numbers, or the field with one element. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The vortex in the north was also found to be surrounded by increasing levels of a certain simple molecule as latitude decreased. This suggests that the vortex is isolating the polar atmosphere from the equatorial atmosphere through a process involving the circulation of air. As a result, the equipment used to study the atmosphere from the Cassini spacecraft is likely underestimating the rates of chemical destruction of this molecule by as much as five times the previously predicted amount. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a massive storm known as the north polar hexagon storm and was shown to play a key role in the formation of the vortex. The vortex in the north is eventually broken down by the flow of warm air caused by the angle of the sun changing at the end of the summer, but it is expected that it will form again in the summer of 2025 due to the 10 and a half earth year solar orbit period of the Saturn system. The Saturn Global Surveyor is one possible spacecraft that could study this phenomenon in more depth in the future. The study presented here provides a comprehensive view of the largest thermal and chemical contrast in the Saturn system and the key factors that influence its formation. The vortex in the north is expected to offer valuable insights into the principles of atmospheric physics and chemistry and could serve as a benchmark for comparing the atmospheres of the other gas giants in the Saturn system and the Jupiter system in the future. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach also allows us to prove a stronger, optimal blow-up criterion for type II solutions. Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the form of a honeycomb lattice. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique filtering effects on the orbits, breaks spatial symmetry, and produces the desired exotic quantum properties. A key characteristic of this system is its large-gap of around 0.36 eV, alongside isolated Dirac cones on the edges which indicate potential applications for room temperature spin-transport. Investigations of the spin Hall conductivity and berry curvatures show high conductivity when compared to other Xene materials. These properties can be quantified with the Z2 invariant and Chern number both being 1. A practical implementation of this is demonstrated in strain engineered hBN/TeO/hBN quantum wells that exhibit a significant non-trivial gap of 0.11 eV. Oxygen functionalization brings robust and stable electronic properties that could facilitate viable spintronic applications despite potential surface oxidation. Further experimental validation is needed to confirm these findings. These predictions showcase the capability of strain engineering Xene materials with potential applications in robust spintronic devices.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The major benefits of our approach include its adaptability to complex mesh configurations, minimal required parameters and the absence of parameter tuning. Furthermore, our approach allows for easier implementation of fracture interaction conditions. A key contribution of this paper is the introduction of screening criteria for fractional flow theory within the same environment. This has resulting in our method being applicable to the simulation of injection and extraction processes within fractured porous media. Ultimately, our approach has the potential to contribute positively to the simulation of greater complexity systems that involve multiple phases and components. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  In addition, we were able to fit our data for the shift in emission line at high temperatures using a combination of the Mott-Seitz model and the Boltzmann distribution, and obtained parameters for the overlap of wave functions, with an energy of about 0.09 electron volts.  We also found that increasing temperature leads to a slowing down of the lattice diamond, as evidenced by a decrease in the lattice contribution to the full width at half maximum of the emission line, from approximately 0.072 degrees Kelvin at room temperature to about 0.026 degrees Kelvin at 500 degrees Kelvin.  We believe that our research will be useful in the development of sensitive magnetic field detectors that operate at high temperatures and in vacuum environments.  Furthermore, we propose that this center may serve as a precise thermometer for monitoring high temperatures in vacuum environments.  In order to determine the stability of the center under continuous optical excitation at high temperatures, we conducted in situ experiments using optical spectroscopy, revealing that the center remains stable at temperatures of up to 500 degrees Kelvin for exposure times of up to 30 minutes.  However, we also observed that increasing temperatures above 500 degrees Kelvin leads to a decrease in the intensity of the emission line, likely due to the presence of optical damage in the diamond.  We were able to improve the stability of the center by reducing the power of the exciting laser, resulting in a reduction of optical damage.  In this study, we used a diamond sample that contained a high concentration of nitrogen-vacancy centers, specifically with a concentration of approximately 5.57 x 10 to the 13th per square inch.  In order to minimize the effects of spectral cross talk between different nitrogen-vacancy centers, we conducted experiments using a high-speed data acquisition system and a lock-in amplifier

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. This implementation facilitates a new approach to analyzing ground states of electron gases confined harmonically, allowing for accurate data extraction regardless of collisionless regime. The algorithm is open-source and freely accessible via the HARmonic Electron calculator web server at the Materials Simulation Society web site. The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems. This also paves the way for implementing robust control measures to manage these systems through managed feedback of their performance data. This is illustrated through a hypothetical example involving the control of an explosive synchronization phenomenon occurring in a neural network. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, we validate our findings numerically with experiments. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. The new example is an (x,y)-bigramian graph of order n, where x and y are close to n/2 and the graph has a high enough girth, but it cannot be colored using the specified distance criterion with a certain number of colors. The number of colors required is similar to the square of the largest component in its automorphism group, especially in catlin trees and some bipartite graphs, but in some cases especially those closely related to Ramanujan graphs, the number of colors required is much lower. The construction of this kind of graph for any given number of colors, but not too low, also provides a lower bound for the number of colors required in its own right. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion.  Ultimately, our study demonstrates that both a viscoelastic medium and asymmetry in the swimmer are necessary for this elasticity-related force to impact swimming speed.  Additionally, our results highlight the significance of the interplay between fluid properties and swimmer design.  To facilitate comparison with theoretical predictions, our study includes detailed measurements of force experienced by the swimmers.  Our data suggests that the elasticity-related force is most pronounced when the viscoelastic force is similar in magnitude to the swimmer experiencing it, suggesting that swimmer design could be optimized for specific fluid properties to maximize its speed.  Overall, our research reveals that viscoelastic forces' effect on swimmer speed is heavily dependent on both the swimmer and its interaction with the surrounding fluid, making it necessary to thoroughly consider the properties of both the swimmer and fluid it is traveling through.  This understanding is critical for the development of efficient swimmers capable of optimizing their performance across various fluid types. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In contrast, many games failed to reach a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "individual learning" algorithms. The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning models 
capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and pinpointing 
embedded security vulnerabilities are needed. Our approach incorporates a 
Bidirectional LSTM model, pre-trained on extensive linguistic data, along with 
a Universal Sentence Encoder to enhance the ISO 27001-compliant security 
ontology. By utilizing a high-performance computing platform to analyze vast 
corpora, we have achieved over 80% accuracy in validating the model's 
robustness and capacity for identifying unseen concepts within the ontology 
and web page instances. Moreover, the inclusion of medical knowledge does 
not compromise the model's performance, showcasing its versatility for applying 
machine learning to multiple domain ontologies. Furthermore, an evaluation 
of the proposed approach on real-world scenarios has demonstrated outstanding 
results, yielding an impressive 85.3% accuracy when validating the model's 
understanding of actual security situations. Consequently, this innovative use 
of Deep Learning paves the way for advancing the interpretation of natural 
language and security ontology, thereby enriching the foundation of threat 
intelligence. Along with the unparalleled performance, our solution provides 
machine learning-based algorithms, encompassing anomaly detection and a 
Unified Sentence Encoder, alongside an ISO 27001-compliant security ontology 
and web page instance codes - all available on GitHub, representing a 
groundbreaking step in the pursuit of combining Deep Learning and cybersecurity.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. These findings are accompanied by an analytical proof that demonstrates even a single Ising agent in a system dominated by voter agents can give rise to a non-zero magnetization in the stationary state. Moreover, this magnetic order becomes more pronounced with an increase in the concentration of Ising agents, ultimately leading to a phase transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic ordering at a specific concentration. This critical concentration represents a novel exponent for the Ising model, determined through numerical simulations as approximately $1.5$. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, we compare our model's predictions to existing research and discuss the implications for infection spread in different environments.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. All code and data are freely accessible at https://github.com/zhuegg/multiling-uws.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Lastly, predicted global elliptic 
vortex potential patterns in QCD are supported by our Xe-Xe collision data. 
Initial results provide significant insights into LHC QCD research and may 
eventually aid in resolving the "constellation problem" in hadron formation. 
Further analysis is needed to thoroughly explore particle properties such as
consistency of spin alignment with respect to the initial intrinsic spin. 
Additionally, our findings highlight the necessity for a comprehensive 
study of strange quark behaviour within the high-energy environment of the
LHC. Lastly, our research paves the way for in-depth investigations of
strangeness in future LHC collisions involving larger nuclear targets. 
Detailed data along with analytical tools are made available to foster
further research into particle property analysis and QCD field theory
aspects.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A tentative proposal is made to amend the model by integrating a new feature that takes into account the influence of transportation systems on the movement of individuals in urban areas. This revised model could provide valuable insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate the spread of violent unrest in densely populated cities. A key methodological innovation involves introducing a new equation that reflects the perceived risks associated with traveling to specific locations, along with corresponding mathematical derivations. The amended model is then applied to Santiago, using data from October 28th, 2019, as a test case. While the revised model shows potential for predicting the peak intensity of rioting in each Santiago subway station with reasonable accuracy, further research is needed to enhance its effectiveness in simulating the actual spread of riots in the city. The amended model is made publicly accessible through a user-friendly web visualizer, offering an interactive platform for users to explore and customize their own urban riot simulation scenarios. The model's source code is also available upon request. The present study represents a initial exploration into modeling the geographical dissemination of intense crowds in densely populated cities and is accompanied by several potential directions for future research. The methods employed in this project can be applied to similar scenarios involving the rapid spread of information and intense movements in compact areas. The project's code, data, and findings are shared with the aim of stimulating discussion and collecting constructive feedback from other researchers. The project's code can be found at https://github.com/AlfonsodeBazala/Riots-EPIDEMIOLOGICAL-MODEL, the data at https://github.com/AlfonsodeBazala/Data-raw, and the model's variations at https://github.com/AlfonsodeBazala/Riots-EPIDEMIOLOGICAL-MODEL- variations. The project's code was developed using Python 3.7, and the results were generated using iPython 3.7. The project's figures were created using Python 3.

Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. However, even with limited observation times, we find that the line can provide valuable constraints on the model's global and local scales, helping to test the model's accuracy across different star formation rates and in different galaxy environments. This could have significant implications for how the model is used in future analyses of spectroscopic data from JWST. Finally, we highlight the potential for observing the line to be a important indicator of star formation rates in galaxies, particularly when combined with other observational evidence, and discuss the need for further research into the relationship between this line and other spectral features. This work also explores the feasibility of using the Prospector framework to predict other quantities, including gas masses and stellar velocities, although the results are more mixed and highlight the need for further research in these areas. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Moreover, the proposed algorithm successfully combines optical flow and inertial information, achieving a notable improvement, demonstrating its capability to effectively utilize different sensing modalities for VIO. The code is available at: https://github.com/heng8/VIO_MMA. The work has been accepted for publication at CVPR 2021.

In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Additionally, we predict that SHOWS will exhibit unique photoemission spectra under linear and circular light sources. Lastly, we propose showbing other topological states, such as nonlinear Majorana modes within SHOWS, with experiments being genuinely feasible with current technology. Overall, this study breaks new ground in nonlinear topological physics and provides concrete proposals for experimental investigations in 3D solid-state systems.
