In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed models also achieve superior performance without additional training data or noise. To further analyze our look-ahead attention model, we conduct a visual analysis of attention on the Chinese-to-English translation task. The results show consistent reductions in confusion between target words. We have released our data and code to facilitate future research. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. The model's viscosity has a minor influence on the development of the cosmos, mainly impacting the galaxy clusters. For the cosmos' future, our predictions indicate that both the model's equation of state and viscosity will continue to have significant impacts. Nevertheless, towards the end of this future period, the cosmos will once again reach a state of stagnation. Consequently, our model predicts that the cosmos will experience 4 more months of stagnation before entering an ultimate acceleration phase. Ultimately, this model has the capability to anticipate the cosmos' evolution through various stages, from its early days through its present phase, and finally in its future. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  We believe that our research will motivate the scientific community to explore the design of computer-supported collaborative learning environments that can identify and respond to student curiosity. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this approach reduces the coverage gap between theoretical maximum coverage and practical coverage by at least 27.2%. Our optimization technique achieves a maximum reliability of at least 27.3% with the routing algorithm, and the fleet size required is comparable to existing ridesharing services, indicating tremendous potential for this mobile sensing approach to become a viable alternative or complement to current urban road sensing practices. As a bonus, our methodology for data analysis also provides valuable insights to transportation authorities and urban planners, enabling more informed decision making about priority road maintenance and optimization of the city's layout. Consequently, this approach has the capability to significantly contribute to better managed and more efficient urban transportation systems. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. We also identified that heavy dark matter beyond the direct detection sensitivity range could also be constrained by J/ψ invisible decays, specifically by 41 GeV for a 1 eV mass scale at the 95% confidence level. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that J/ψ decay into a neutrino and a photon can provide competing limits on certain effective operators, particularly for heavy neutrinos with masses ranging from 10-100 GeV, with additional constraints on specific operator combinations that arise from considering both invisible and radiative decays of the J/ψ particle. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we show that our new methods have similar order conditions to their uniform stepsize counterparts, and this development provides a starting point for further exploring methods on non-uniform grids.

We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Our findings are relevant not only to the specific autoscoring models investigated but also to any other scoring systems developed using similar techniques. Furthermore, our detection-based protection solutions are applicable to a broad range of other sensitive machine learning models that are difficult to understand and analyze. We have made the code and data associated with this research publicly available. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the W-shaped network is designed as a nested, bi-directional neural network. By operating on density masks, which represent the density and shape of objects rather than their exact position, the model is better equipped to handle variations in the positions of nuclei within an image. To further enhance the model's performance, it's trained on synthetic density masks generated by modifying actual density masks, thus increasing its ability to detect a range of different nucleus shapes. In tests on two public datasets, the W-shaped network demonstrated a significant improvement in nucleus detection accuracy, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art point-based detection models. Furthermore, the model's density mask output contains valuable diagnostic information for autopathology tasks, demonstrating its potential as a reliable alternative to traditional mask-based nucleus segmentation methods. In addition to evaluating the model's performance on synthetic density masks, it was also tested on actual density masks extracted from density masks generated by pathologists, yielding comparable results to existing nucleus segmentation methods. In conclusion, the proposed W-shaped network, a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm, has achieved outstanding performance on the MDA-ND and NDSC datasets, outperforming point-based detection models, demonstrating its potential as a reliable method for cancer diagnosis. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. Through this combined effort, we aim to explore the cell death pathways underlying COVID-19's severe complications. By doing so, we may be able to pinpoint key cellular targets for treatment, especially in cases where inflammation is a major concern. Ultimately, this research seeks to advance our understanding of the cellular mechanisms underlying pyroptosis in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection, with the ultimate goal of informing potential therapeutic strategies. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. However, the results are sensitive to the choice of parameter values. The proposed approaches could provide a framework for a broader understanding of the role of variable selection in reinforcement learning, encompassing topics such as the identification of redundant state variables and the concept of state variable hierarchies. This research offers a initial exploration of these concepts, and various questions remain unanswered to justify further investigation. The associated code is freely accessible and enables the replication of results and the exploration of novel concepts across a broad range of reinforcement learning applications. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Our research offers a comprehensive, unified explanation of GCNNs and serves as a comprehensive guide for educators to effectively teach GCNNs in the classroom. It also provides valuable insights for practitioners to make informed decisions when employing GCNNs for real-world applications. All necessary material, including detailed notes and accompanying numerical/visual examples, has been made freely accessible to support the publication's findings. Additionally, we introduce a novel, simplified representation of GCNNs, encompassing multi-dimensional data architectures, designed to facilitate the clear exposition of deep learning concepts. This novel representation can also serve as a useful tool for the interactive exploration of complex deep learning topics. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Additionally, simulation outcomes demonstrate the technique's ability to estimate mechanical properties, including Young's modulus and chord modulus, providing the foundation for its potential applications in elastography. The proposed VSSA beamforming technique facilitates a notable increase in lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, enabling accurate estimation of lateral tissue displacement and tissue mechanical properties. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that incorporating deeper neural networks for player policies yields superior performance across both the micro and macro grids levels. Our method's effectiveness is further highlighted by low policy compression sizes, achieving highly competitive compression ratios in comparison to flat PEGs. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/ruipg/hierPEG. Our framework offers a valuable resource for investigating grid world games through large-scale experimental designs. It also provides a computational precedent that can be adapted for other complex decision-making applications.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

Additionally, our work involves an exploration of 'nontransitive' triples, where the relationship between the components' probabilities diverges. We identify the specific conditions under which the middle component's probability increases towards 1, as well as the distribution associated with the smallest component when the largest component's probability approaches 0. Our research also provides a comparison of the probabilities associated with the smallest and largest components in a 'nontransitive' triple, and establishes the specific condition under which the largest component's probability surpasses 0.5. 

Our study provides an extension to existing knowledge on counterintuitive phenomena, and highlights the distinct characteristics that distinguish 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' triples. We also introduce new problems related to the evaluation of counterfactual probabilities within these contexts. 

Finally, we derive upper and lower limits for the probability of selecting a 'nontransitive' triple, and establish the probability distribution associated with the middle component in this context. Our research provides an exploration of generalizing these concepts across different probability scales. 

Our analysis is accompanied by numerical evaluations

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed architecture achieves greater flexibility, enabling the enhancement of various CT images with different doses, such as from low-dose to routine-dose and cancer-radiation dose reduction, without needing to adjust the network architecture. Furthermore, by leveraging the switchable nature of the generator, we developed an intuitive interactive method for patients and radiologists to co-adapt the dose enhancement, allowing for more precise control over the output images. Our method outperformed state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for low-dose CT image denoising, both subjectively and objectively, and successfully handled non-uniform noise by incorporating the use of a noise reduction module. Finally, we successfully applied our proposed architecture in a real-world clinical setting. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our approach demonstrates the potential to solve complex inverse problems by leveraging the capacity of deep neural networks to model intricate patterns in data. It also addresses a major limitation of the GAN field, which has been criticized for lacking theoretical robustness, by incorporating a regularized formulation that ensures the posterior samples' diversity and adherence to defined constraints. This technique can be interpreted as implementing a penalty method for the CWGAN trainer. We provided a numerically efficient solution to the inverse problem by having the GAN enforce the prior distribution, thereby bypassing the need for drawing massive datasets. We offered a simplified implementation for generating samples from the posterior distribution in a collaborative MRI example. Interestingly, our approach also offers an alternative to traditional sampling methods such as Monte Carlo, by allowing for the generation of an unlimited number of samples given a sufficient number of training iterations. This capability could lead to the development of new algorithms that take advantage of the inherent efficiency of iteratively refining the sampling process. We open-sourced our code on GitHub in an effort to facilitate a discussion on this topic. Feedback is welcome. Reply to comments will be included in a revised version of this paper. 

Keywords: Inverse problems, Sampling from the posterior distribution, GAN, MRI, Image processing, Inference. 

This work has been accepted for oral presentation at the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Pattern Analysis, Barcelona, Spain, July 2022. 

Note: This work has been presented in an earlier form at the 31st British Machine Vision Conference, September 2017, Gloucester, UK. However, significant advancements have been made since then, particularly in the GAN-based approach, which is the focus of the current work.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The screen at about 20 AU in radius fills the line of sight to the pulsar, and its velocity is consistent with the flow pattern seen in neutral gas as observed in Lyman-alpha spectra. The results also show that the scintillation patterns produce suitable conditions for the formation of pulsar channeling, which could explain the beamed radio emission from the pulsar. Furthermore, the screen associated with the void in the direction of the Sco-Cen association may contribute to the observed variations in scintillation patterns of pulsars in that region. The findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 and their effects on the pulsar's radio emission. The method employed in this research can be applied to a broader range of screens and pulsars to gain insight into the interstellar medium. The screens identified in this study will continue to be monitored for changes, which can provide information on the velocity and structure of the screens, as well as the effects of high-energy particle flows and other phenomena on the interstellar medium. The data collected over several decades also offers the opportunity to detect possible instabilities in the screens and their impact on the surrounding environment. The research presented here is a initial outcome of a long-term project to systematically study screens in the line of sight to pulsars through scintillation observations. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, a subjective test confirms that QPNet can generate clinically relevant speech with a natural quality. The source codes for this work have been made available online for the community's reference.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN succeeds in generating hierarchical graphs from random data, and it achieves better performance than existing methods on noisy graphs. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

Furthermore, we found that the D-poor water with hydrogen isotopic values ranging from -444 to -56.9 originated from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that this water could serve as a distinct water reservoir with lower D isotope values compared to the water with high D isotope values found in chondrites and incorporated into the terrestrial planets. This new water reservoir can help explain the observed variation in the D isotope values of the water on Earth and also provides a new perspective on the delivery of water to the terrestrial planets during planetary accretion. 

In addition, our research offered a new perspective on the formation of chondrite matrices by showing that the D-poor hydrogen isotopic values of organic carbonates in the Anandallas and Anouk chondrites could indicate the presence of a distinct volatile-rich gas phase in the Solar System birthplace. This distinct gas phase may have originated from the evolution of the Solar System baby disk during the phase of chaotic accretion. The legacy of this volatile-rich gas phase can still be seen in the varying D isotope values of the water on Earth today.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the benefits of zero-shot learning for speech-to-text in new language pairs. We also observe the advantages of our approaches for languages with limited available data, notably for Vietnamese. To facilitate future research, we release our code, pre-trained models, and data, thereby providing a foundation for the development of more efficient zero-shot speech-to-text models. Lastly, we anticipate that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of zero-shot learning in speech-to-text and encourage the community to explore and improve upon our results. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The framework we introduce also enables a new approach to extracting interaction strengths and spin-orbit coupling constants from experimental data, an option we demonstrate through a renowned example, the phase diagram of $RuO_2$. Finally, our study prompts a review of previous theoretical work on magnetic properties in $RuO_2$, highlighting the importance of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing and suggesting potential paths for further research and experimentation.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. The study also reveals limitations of the proposed relative I-function properties in certain scenarios. Furthermore, it establishes a direct connection between quantum cohomology and another mathematical theory, known as mirror symmetry, in a particular computational scenario. The computation involves a family of Calabi-Yau manifolds that are parameterized by modifying the weights of a certain mathematical vector, and demonstrates that this family exhibits a desired property known as stability. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is delivered via a user
friendly graphical interface built with JavaFX, making it an independent,
platform-independent tool that can be used on Windows, Linux, and macOS
operating systems. The application is accompanied by a comprehensive set of
methods for data analysis, described in detail in the user guide available at

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments.
